examples.everyday: My friend who works at an AI startup says their chatbot got better after they switched to direct preference optimization.
examples.professional: Let's run the next fine-tuning job with direct preference optimization and compare the win rate against last week's RLHF baseline.
examples.analytical: Direct preference optimization reframes alignment as a classification problem over preference pairs, so the policy is learned without an explicit reward model.

nuance.analogy: It is like learning which of two dishes a customer liked more, instead of first writing a detailed scoring rubric and then cooking to it.
nuance.etymology: Built from the English words direct, preference, and optimization; the method was named in a 2023 paper.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on DI-rect instead of on the final -ZAY- syllable of optimization
Confusing preference optimization with reinforcement learning in general; DPO is a specific, simpler method

conversation.text: Direct preference optimization trains on preference pairs directly, with no separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.
Direct preference optimization is simpler to implement and often more stable than PPO-based RLHF.
We fine-tune with direct preference optimization, using the SFT model as the reference policy.

senses.definition: Causing discomfort.

core.definition: Causing a feeling of unease, mild pain, or emotional discomfort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DIS. The second syllable, kum, has a short u, and the final -ing is a light, unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It describes something that makes people uneasy, whether physically or emotionally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discomforting in written reports, news, and careful speech about unpleasant facts or symptoms. In casual conversation people more often say uncomfortable or awkward. It is less intense than alarming and softer than disturbing.

distinctions.note: Uncomfortable is the everyday word and can describe either physical seats or social situations, while discomforting is more formal and often describes an effect on someone.
Disconcerting implies surprise and loss of composure, whereas discomforting suggests a more steady, ongoing unease.
Disturbing is stronger and implies distress or moral shock, while discomforting is milder.

examples.everyday: It was a little discomforting to hear the doctor say the test results needed a second look.
examples.professional: The discomforting trend in our churn data suggests that customers are leaving before the onboarding is complete.
examples.analytical: The argument is discomforting because it implies that moral certainty may conceal a deeper form of self-deception.

nuance.analogy: A discomforting thought is like a stone in your shoe: it doesn't stop you, but you can't stop noticing it.
nuance.etymology: From discomfort plus the suffix -ing, forming an adjective describing an effect.
common_mistakes: Confusing discomforting with discomfiting, which means embarrassing or defeating.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: A Protestant evangelical theology dividing history into distinct periods (dispensations, rooted in the writings of John Nelson Darby).

core.definition: A Protestant evangelical theology that divides history into distinct periods, or dispensations, in which God deals with humanity under different arrangements.

pronunciation.tip: Stress shifts to the -ism: LIZ, with secondary stress on 'say'. Say the -ism ending as a reduced 'um', and do not drop the schwa in 'shuh-nuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship; supporters see it as faithful to Scripture, critics see it as artificial or divisive.
nuance.usage_note: Systematized by John Nelson Darby in the 1800s and popularized in the US by the Scofield Reference Bible and later works such as the Left Behind novels. Americans use it in discussions of evangelicalism, prophecy, and Israel policy. Say 'a dispensationalist' for an adherent.

distinctions.note: Covenant theology organizes Scripture by covenants and sees one people of God, while dispensationalism distinguishes Israel and the church.
Premillennialism is a view about Christ's return before the millennium; dispensationalism is a broader interpretive system that usually includes it.
Fundamentalism is a broad movement defending traditional doctrines; dispensationalism is one specific theology many fundamentalists hold.

examples.everyday: My aunt grew up in a church that taught dispensationalism, so she knows the whole timeline of the end times.
examples.professional: The professor assigned a chapter on dispensationalism before our discussion of American evangelical politics.
examples.analytical: Progressive dispensationalism softens the classical separation of Israel and the church, yet it retains a distinct role for national Israel.

nuance.analogy: It treats history like a play in several acts, each with different rules for the cast.
nuance.etymology: From dispensation (Latin dispensatio, 'distribution, management') plus -al and -ism.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'DIS' instead of the -ism syllable.
Treating it as a general word for dispensing or distributing.
Confusing it with 'dispensing' in pharmacy.
nuance.biblical_note: Dispensationalists build on Greek oikonomia ('stewardship, administration') in Ephesians 1:10 and 3:2, which speak of God's administration of grace. They also point to divisions such as the covenants with Abraham and Moses (Genesis 12; Exodus 19-20) and the new covenant announced in Jeremiah 31:31-34.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy does not teach dispensationalism and sees one continuous divine economy culminating in Christ and the Church, with no separate earthly destiny for Israel.
The Catholic Church sees a single plan of salvation with the Church as the new Israel, and rejects the dispensationalist rapture and separate-plans scheme.

It arose among Plymouth Brethren and spread among American Baptists, Bible churches, and many Pentecostals. Reformed, Lutheran, and Anglican theologians mostly reject it in favor of covenantal approaches.

senses.definition: Having a bad or foul taste.
senses.example: The food had very distasteful flavor.

senses.definition: Unpleasant.
senses.example: Scrubbing the floors was a distasteful duty to perform.

senses.definition: Offensive.
senses.example: distasteful language

core.definition: Unpleasant or offensive, especially in a way that causes disapproval or disgust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the -ful ending is reduced to a short ful sound. Say the st cluster clearly, but do not add an extra vowel between the s and t.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses clear disapproval, often of behavior, jokes, or actions rather than food alone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use distasteful for jokes, behavior, or comments that are offensive or inappropriate, and sometimes for food with an unpleasant flavor. It is more polite than disgusting and more formal than gross. In casual speech, people often say that was in poor taste or that's gross.

distinctions.note: Tasteless often means lacking good taste or style; distasteful focuses on something unpleasant or offensive to the person experiencing it.
Disgusting is stronger and more physical; distasteful is milder and often used for behavior or ideas.

examples.everyday: I thought that joke at dinner was really distasteful, and I wish you hadn't told it in front of my kids.
examples.professional: The ad was distasteful to our customers, so marketing pulled it before the campaign launched.
examples.analytical: Kant would argue that an action can be distasteful without being wrong, because disgust does not always track moral duty.

nuance.analogy: Something distasteful is like a sour note in a sweet dessert: it spoils the whole experience.
nuance.etymology: From distaste, from dis- (not) and taste, combined with the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using distasteful only for food, when it is very common for behavior, comments, or ideas.
Confusing distasteful with distasteful's root distaste, which is a noun.

senses.definition: That which distinguishes; a single occurrence of a determining factor or feature, the fact of being divided; separation, discrimination.
The act of distinguishing, discriminating; discrimination.
senses.example: There is a distinction to be made between resting and slacking.

senses.definition: A feature that causes someone or something to stand out from others of its type.
senses.example: She had the distinction of meeting the Queen.

senses.definition: A feature that causes someone or something to stand out as being better; a mark of honor, rank, eminence or excellence; the quality of being distinguished.
senses.example: She had the distinction of meeting the Queen.

senses.definition: Punctuation or typographical marks.

core.definition: A clear difference between things, or an honor or quality that makes someone stand out from others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on 'STINGK'. The 'nk' is pronounced together, and the 'ct' sound is written but the final syllable is simply 'shun'. Keep the first vowel reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means excellence or honor; neutral when it means a difference or a line drawn between things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'make a distinction' when separating ideas, as in 'make a distinction between facts and opinions'. For a personal honor, people say 'the distinction of' or 'with distinction', for example graduating with distinction. In casual speech people more often say 'difference'.

distinctions.note: 'Difference' is the everyday word for any way things are not the same. 'Distinction' is more precise and often suggests a meaningful line drawn between concepts.
'Honor' means respect or a prize given to someone. 'Distinction' can mean an achievement that sets someone apart, but it is less ceremonial.

examples.everyday: My brother graduated from college with distinction, and our whole family was proud of him.
examples.professional: Before we write the report, we need to make a clear distinction between the two sources of error.
examples.analytical: Aristotle draws an important distinction between potentiality and actuality in his metaphysics.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence line that separates one field from the next, so each thing is clearly on its own side.
nuance.etymology: From Latin distinctio, from distinguere, 'to separate, mark off'.
common_mistakes: Using 'distinction' where 'difference' is more natural in casual talk.
Saying 'distinction with' instead of 'with distinction' for an honor.

distinction.etymology: From Middle English *distinccioun*, from Old French *distinction* (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin *distinctio*, action noun of *distinguō* (“separate, distinguish”).

senses.definition: Having a quality that divides or separates.
senses.example: Rather than fostering unity, he becomes divisive.

core.definition: Tending to cause disagreement, conflict or division among people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VY. The final -ive is pronounced "iv," with a short i, not "eve."

nuance.connotation: Negative; describes issues or rhetoric that split groups, though the speaker may consider the division necessary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use divisive frequently in political, social and workplace discussions, for example "a divisive issue" or "a divisive candidate." It is neutral to slightly negative and is often used to describe topics people argue about rather than people themselves. In casual conversation you might hear "touchy" or "polarizing," which feel more informal.

distinctions.note: Polarizing describes something that pushes people to opposite extremes; divisive emphasizes the splitting of a group into factions.
Controversial means causing public debate; divisive stresses that the debate splits people into groups or damages relationships.

examples.everyday: Let's not bring up politics at dinner, because it always gets divisive with my brother.
examples.professional: The proposal for a new reporting structure proved divisive among the engineering teams.
examples.analytical: Her argument that the sacraments belong to the whole church, not to one party, is deliberately unifying rather than divisive.

nuance.analogy: A divisive issue is like a fault line in the ground: it runs through the group and can split it apart when pressure builds.
nuance.etymology: From Latin divisivus, from dividere (to divide).
common_mistakes: Using divisive to mean simply difficult or hard; it specifically means causing division between people.
Pronouncing it as dih-VIE-siv with a long final vowel.
Confusing divisive with divisible, which means able to be divided.

do-you-know-when-it'll-be-back-in-stock.phonetic: /du ju ˌnoʊ ˌwɛn ˌɪtəl bi ˌbæk ɪn ˈstɑk/

senses.definition: Asking when a sold-out item will be available again.

core.definition: Asking when a sold-out item will be available to buy again from the store.

pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo KNOH when IT-ul bee BAK in STAHK
pronunciation.tip: The stress usually falls on 'know', 'back' and 'stock', while 'it'll' and 'in' are reduced. 'It'll' sounds like 'IT-ul', and 'when' and 'will' sound like 'wen' and 'wil' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: neutral and polite. It shows interest in the product without complaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this at a store counter, on the phone, or on a retailer's website chat. Use it when a size or product is sold out and you want to know if it will be restocked. Typical replies are 'We're expecting a shipment next week' or 'I can put you on the waitlist'. Asking for a waitlist or a notification is also common in online shopping.

distinctions.note: A yes/no question about current availability; the question here asks about the future.
Also natural and direct; the question in this entry is more polite and uses the phrase 'back in stock'.

collocations: notify me when it's back in stock

examples.everyday: Do you know when it'll be back in stock? My daughter really wants this one for her birthday.
examples.professional: Do you know when the replacement parts will be back in stock? Our repair queue is growing.
examples.analytical: Customers who ask when an item will be back in stock are signaling demand, which a retailer can use to forecast reorders.

nuance.analogy: Like a theater ticket that is sold out: you want to know when a new batch will go on sale.
nuance.etymology: Stock comes from Old English stocc, meaning 'tree trunk' or 'block', and later came to mean goods held for sale.
common_mistakes: Using inverted word order in the indirect question: say 'when it'll be' rather than 'when will it be'.
Saying 'back to stock' instead of 'back in stock'.

conversation.text: Do you know when it'll be back in stock? I need it for a party.

senses.definition: An authoritative principle, belief or statement of opinion, especially one considered to be absolutely true and indisputable, regardless of evidence or without evidence to support it.
A doctrine (or set of doctrines) relating to matters such as morality and faith, set forth authoritatively by a religious organization or leader.
senses.example: In the Catholic Church, new dogmas can only be declared by the pope after the extremely rare procedure ex cathedra to make them part of the official faith.

core.definition: A belief or set of beliefs officially declared by a religious authority as true and binding; also, any belief held rigidly without question.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'a' is a weak 'uh', not a full 'ah'. The 'g' is pronounced, so it is not 'dog-ma' with a silent g.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in everyday speech, suggesting rigid, unquestioned belief; neutral or positive in Catholic theology.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'dogma' usually criticizes closed-minded thinking, as in 'political dogma'. In Catholic and Orthodox theology it is a technical term for a defined truth of faith. The adjective 'dogmatic' is usually an insult.

distinctions.note: Doctrine is a broader teaching, whereas dogma is a doctrine declared binding on all members.
A creed is a formal statement of belief; a dogma is one specific defined truth.
Orthodoxy means accepted or correct belief overall; a dogma is a single item within it.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of arguing with him; he treats every opinion he has like dogma.
examples.professional: We should test that assumption instead of treating it as dogma in our modeling process.
examples.analytical: In Catholic theology, a dogma is a truth divinely revealed and infallibly defined by the Church, such as the Trinity.

nuance.analogy: Dogma is like a fence around a field of belief that no one is permitted to cross.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dogma, 'opinion, decree', from dokein, 'to seem good, think'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'a' as 'ah'.
Confusing it with 'dogmatic', the adjective.
Assuming it always means something negative; in theology it is technical.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek dogma means 'decree' and appears in Luke 2:1 (Caesar's decree), Acts 16:4 (the decisions reached by the Jerusalem council), and Ephesians 2:15 (the law with its commandments and ordinances).

traditions.view: Dogmas are the truths of faith defined by the seven ecumenical councils, such as the Trinity and the two natures of Christ. They are received as expressions of the Church's unchanging faith, not new developments.

A dogma is a truth divinely revealed and defined by the Church's teaching authority, requiring assent. Dogmas can be defined by councils or the pope speaking ex cathedra, for example the Immaculate Conception.

Protestants generally use 'dogma' less and root authority in Scripture alone, though they affirm core creedal doctrines like the Trinity. The word often carries a negative sense of unquestioned human tradition.

dogma.etymology: From Latin *dogma* (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek *δόγμα* (“opinion, tenet”), from *δοκέω* (“to seem good, think”).

senses.definition: A system in which typechecking is performed at run time and not at compilation, opposed to static typing.

core.definition: A programming language feature where variable types are checked while the program runs, not before it is compiled.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'TY' in 'typing', while 'dy' gets a lighter secondary stress. Say 'TY-ping' with a clear long i, not 'TIP-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a design choice, with trade-offs rather than a value judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the US use the phrase in technical discussions of languages such as Python, JavaScript or Ruby. It is often contrasted with static typing, and debates about it come up in code reviews and design meetings. Outside tech, the phrase is rarely used, so you would say 'the language checks types as it runs' in a general explanation.

distinctions.note: Static typing checks variable types before the program runs, while dynamic typing checks them during execution.
Weak typing describes how freely a language converts between types, while dynamic typing is about when types are checked.

examples.everyday: My cousin is learning to code, and she said Python uses dynamic typing, so the types are checked as the program runs.
examples.professional: We chose a dynamically typed language for the prototype, but we will add type hints before the production release.
examples.analytical: Proponents of dynamic typing argue that flexibility speeds early development, while critics say it moves error detection to runtime.

nuance.analogy: Dynamic typing is like checking a passport at the gate instead of at the airport counter; the check happens at the moment of use.
nuance.etymology: 'Dynamic' from Greek dynamikos, 'powerful', and 'typing' from Greek typos, 'impression' or 'form'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'DY-namic' too heavily, which makes the rhythm sound off.
Confusing dynamic typing with weakly typed languages.
Saying 'dynamic type' when the usual phrase is 'dynamic typing'.

senses.definition: To solve, write or compose by working studiously at night; to study.

core.definition: To work studiously late into the night, especially to write, compose, or solve something; to study intensely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, LOO. The middle syllables are quick and unstressed, and the final 'ate' is a clear 'ayt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly admiring. It describes diligent, lamp-lit labor, often with a hint of old-fashioned scholarship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use elucidate's rare cousin elucubrate in speech. You will meet it in old essays, literary prose, or deliberately antique writing, and it signals a bookish, learned tone. In modern American English, say 'work late on' or 'burn the midnight oil' instead.

distinctions.note: Study is the ordinary word for learning; elucubrate specifically suggests late-night, painstaking work by lamplight.
Elucidate means to make clear; elucubrate means to labor over something, and the two are easily confused by learners.

examples.everyday: My grandfather would elucubrate over his ledgers at the kitchen table until midnight.
examples.professional: I elucubrated over the proof until two in the morning, so the slides are rough but the math is sound.
examples.analytical: Medieval scholars elucubrated over glosses that later readers found nearly impenetrable.

nuance.analogy: To elucubrate is to be the one still awake under a desk lamp while the rest of the house sleeps.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elucubrare, 'to work by lamplight', from lucubrum 'lamplight', related to lux 'light'.
common_mistakes: Confusing elucubrate with elucidate; they sound alike but mean very different things.
Using it in casual conversation, where it sounds old-fashioned and pretentious.

elucubrate.etymology: From the past participle of Latin *elucubrare* (“compose by lamplight”).

senses.definition: Inspiring affection or love, often in a childlike way.
Synonym of endearment.

core.definition: Causing people to feel affection for someone, often because of charm, warmth or innocence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, DEER. The r is clear in American speech, and the final -ing is a light 'ing' sound, not 'een'.

nuance.connotation: positive. It describes a quality that makes people fond of someone, though it can sound patronizing if used for an adult's effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use endearing for a child's habits, a pet, a clumsy but kind friend, or a quirky personality. It is warm and friendly, and it fits casual conversation and written reviews. Saying 'That's endearing' can sound slightly condescending if the person is trying hard and failing.

distinctions.note: Lovable describes a general quality of being easy to love, while endearing focuses on a specific trait that makes someone seem sweet or charming.
Charming suggests polished social appeal, whereas endearing suggests a more innocent or unguarded warmth.

examples.everyday: Our toddler keeps giving the dog his shoes, and it's the most endearing thing ever.
examples.professional: Her endearing habit of thanking every team member made the retrospective feel much less tense.
examples.analytical: The novel's most endearing character is also its most morally uncertain one.

nuance.analogy: Like a puppy who trips over its own paws and makes you want to pick it up.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'endear', from 'en-' and 'dear'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective endearing with the noun endearment, which means an affectionate word or phrase.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'en-DEER-ing' instead of 'in-DEER-ing'.

senses.definition: To conceive or see something within one's mind. To imagine.

core.definition: To picture something in your mind, especially a future possibility or goal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VIZH. The final syllable is weak and sounds like 'un', not 'eye-zhun'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests thoughtful planning or hopeful imagination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use envision in business, planning and personal goals, such as 'I envision a team that meets weekly.' It is slightly more formal than imagine. A natural reply is 'That sounds great' or 'Tell me more about that.'

distinctions.note: Imagine is more general and can refer to fantasy; envision often refers to a planned or hoped-for future.
Envisage is the same in meaning but is more formal and more common in British writing.

examples.everyday: I can envision us living near the lake someday.
examples.professional: I envision a dashboard that updates the model's accuracy every hour for the operations team.
examples.analytical: The theologian envisions creation as an ongoing gift rather than a single past event.

nuance.analogy: Like a mental preview of a movie before it is filmed.
nuance.etymology: From en- 'make' and vision, from Latin visio, a seeing.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pronunciation with 'en-VISH-un'; the s is pronounced like the s in measure.
Using envision for trivial mental pictures; it works best for future possibilities.

envision.etymology: From *en* + *vision*, from Latin *visionem* (“a thing or sight seen”).

senses.definition: The doctrine that consciousness, mental states and processes are simply by-products of physiological events in the brain or nervous system and cannot themselves cause anything, whether material or immaterial.
senses.example: In the eyes of epiphenomenalism, anger does not cause one to shout nor does grief cause one to cry; the feelings are by-products of the underlying physical causes and nothing more.

senses.definition: Such a doctrine, as advanced by a particular thinker or school of thought.

core.definition: The philosophical doctrine that mental states and consciousness are by-products of brain processes and cannot cause physical or other events.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on LIH, the seventh syllable, with secondary stress on the earlier syllables. Keep the vowels reduced in the middle, and don't add an extra syllable before -ism.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in philosophy of mind and sounds scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: In American philosophy departments, epiphenomenalism comes up in debates about consciousness and the mind-body problem. Americans usually discuss it in seminars, books, and papers, not in everyday talk. Thomas Huxley is famously associated with an early form of it, and you may hear that name in classes on the history of philosophy.

distinctions.note: Dualism holds that mind and body are distinct substances, while epiphenomenalism holds that mind is real but has no causal power over the body.
Physicalism says everything is physical; epiphenomenalism can accept physical causes but denies mental states any causal role.
Interactionism holds that mental states cause physical events; epiphenomenalism denies this.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor argued for epiphenomenalism, and at first it sounded crazy to me.
examples.professional: Treating user sentiment as an epiphenomenon of clicks is a kind of epiphenomenalism that ignores its effect on churn.
examples.analytical: Epiphenomenalism holds that consciousness has no causal power, a thesis that threatens the common sense claim that pain makes us withdraw.

nuance.analogy: Like the whistle of a steam train: the steam makes it whistle, but the whistle does not pull the train.
nuance.etymology: From epiphenomenon, from Greek epi- 'upon' and phainomenon 'appearing,' with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing epiphenomenalism, the theory, with epiphenomenon, the thing it describes.
Mispronouncing the word with extra syllables or stress on the wrong part.

senses.definition: To show or illustrate by example.
To be an instance of or serve as an example.
To make an attested copy or transcript of (a document) under seal.
To prove by such an attested copy or transcript.

core.definition: To show or illustrate something by giving an example, or to be a typical example of something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable (ZEM). The middle syllable is a reduced uh, and the final -fy is pronounced like fie. Many learners add an extra syllable in the middle, so keep it to three syllables.

nuance.connotation: positive. It usually suggests that someone or something represents a quality well.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exemplify in professional, academic, and formal writing, and sometimes in speech when they want to sound precise. In casual talk, people more often say show or be an example of. Saying someone exemplifies honesty is a compliment.

distinctions.note: Illustrate means to make something clearer with pictures, examples, or explanation; exemplify puts more weight on being a model or instance of the quality itself.
Embody suggests giving concrete form to an idea or quality, often in a person; exemplify is more about serving as a clear example of it.

examples.everyday: Maria always stays calm when the kids are fighting, and she really exemplifies patience.
examples.professional: Our new onboarding process exemplifies the kind of clear documentation we want on every team.
examples.analytical: Job's endurance in the face of suffering exemplifies a faith that does not require the removal of pain.

nuance.analogy: A flagship store that shows what the whole brand stands for.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin exemplificare, to illustrate by example.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition, as in exemplify of; the verb takes a direct object.
Saying exemplify as an adjective-like word; use exemplary for that meaning.

exemplify.etymology: From Middle English *exemplifien*, from Middle French *exemplifier* and its etymon Medieval Latin *exemplificō*, from Latin *exemplum* (“example”).

senses.definition: To praise; to make high.

core.definition: To praise someone or something enthusiastically, often publicly or in formal language.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STOHL. The first syllable is a reduced ik, and the final l is a clear dark l.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests high, sincere, sometimes elaborate praise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extol mainly in writing, speeches, reviews, or formal tributes, not in casual conversation. In everyday speech they would say praise, rave about, or speak highly of. It can sound stiff in a text message but fits an award speech or a eulogy.

distinctions.note: Praise is everyday and neutral; extol is more formal and emphasizes lofty, enthusiastic praise.
Laud is also formal and often appears in religious or ceremonial language; extol is more general.

collocations: extol the virtues of hard work

examples.everyday: My mom is always extolling the virtues of her new air fryer.
examples.professional: In her review, the director extolled the team's disciplined approach to testing.
examples.analytical: The essay extols the virtues of humility while questioning the rhetoric of public heroism.

nuance.analogy: Like lifting something up on a pedestal so everyone can see it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extollere, to lift up, from ex- (up) and tollere (to lift).
common_mistakes: Using extol with a preposition like extol about; use extol directly with the object.
Confusing extol with extort, which is a different verb about taking money by force.

senses.definition: A statistical method used to describe variability among observed correlated variables in terms of one or more unobserved variables (called factors).
A statistical study performed using the method.

core.definition: A statistical method that identifies a smaller number of hidden factors that explain patterns of correlation among many observed variables.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on NAL in 'analysis', and the final syllable is a short 'sis', not 'sus'. The first word has a secondary stress on FAK, and the 'or' is reduced to 'er'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a precise technical method with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science, psychology, and social science, researchers say 'factor analysis' in papers, reports, and meetings. Be careful to distinguish exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, which are often named explicitly. In casual talk it is rarely mentioned, and people say 'we ran a factor analysis' when discussing a survey.

distinctions.note: PCA finds directions of maximum variance with no latent model, while factor analysis assumes unobserved latent factors cause the correlations.
Cluster analysis groups observations or variables into distinct clusters; factor analysis reduces variables to underlying latent dimensions.

examples.everyday: My sister is doing her thesis, and she spent all weekend on a factor analysis of her survey.
examples.professional: Before we build the churn model, let's run a factor analysis to reduce the twenty customer survey items to a few key drivers.
examples.analytical: Spearman's early factor analysis of mental tests suggested a general intelligence factor underlying diverse cognitive abilities.

nuance.analogy: Factor analysis is like hearing a choir and inferring the few hidden voices that together produce all the harmonies you hear.
nuance.etymology: From Latin factor, 'maker or doer', combined with the Greek analysis, 'a breaking up or loosening'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'factor analyze' as a verb phrase instead of 'run a factor analysis' or 'perform factor analysis'.
Stressing the final syllable of 'analysis' as in 'uh-NAL-uh-SUS'.

senses.definition: Without fault; free from defect or error.
senses.example: faultless effort

core.definition: Completely free from mistakes, defects, or flaws.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FAULT. The last syllable is a reduced 'lus' sound, like 'lis,' not 'lace.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as perfect or nearly perfect, though it can sound a little exaggerated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faultless' more in writing and formal speech than in casual talk. People might describe a performance, a record, or a manner as faultless, as in 'a faultless presentation.' In everyday conversation, 'perfect' or 'flawless' is more common.

distinctions.note: Flawless is more common in everyday American speech and is often used for appearance or skill, while faultless sounds more formal or literary.
Perfect is the broadest word and can be used casually, while faultless emphasizes the absence of errors in conduct or work.

examples.everyday: Her cake was faultless, so everyone asked for the recipe.
examples.professional: The team delivered a faultless release, with no bugs reported in the first week.
examples.analytical: The argument is persuasive, but it is not faultless, since its second premise assumes what it needs to prove.

nuance.analogy: A faultless diamond has no cracks or spots, so every part of it catches the light cleanly.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'fault' (from Old French faute) and the suffix '-less.'
common_mistakes: Using 'faultless' for a person's blame, when 'faultless' means having no errors, not being blameless.
Confusing it with 'faulty,' which means having defects.

senses.definition: Metaphysics.

core.definition: Aristotle's name for metaphysics, the study of being as being and of the first principles that underlie all other sciences.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH in philosophy, and the first syllable reduces to a schwa, so it sounds like fuh-LAH-suh-fee. Keep the r in first and the three-syllable ending clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase almost only in philosophy courses and scholarly writing on Aristotle. In everyday American speech people just say metaphysics. You would seldom hear it outside a classroom or a book.

distinctions.note: Metaphysics is the common modern term for the field; first philosophy is Aristotle's own label for it and stresses its priority over other sciences.
Ontology studies what exists and its categories; first philosophy is broader, also covering the principles that ground all knowledge.

examples.everyday: My roommate is taking a philosophy class and says Aristotle called metaphysics first philosophy, which sounds odd to me.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper, I'll explain how first philosophy differs from the empirical sciences that depend on it.
examples.analytical: For Aristotle, first philosophy studies being qua being, and its dignity lies in its priority over the particular sciences.

nuance.analogy: Like the foundation under a building: every floor depends on it, though people rarely look at it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek prōtē philosophia, 'first philosophy', Aristotle's own name for the science of being.
common_mistakes: Taking first philosophy to mean the first lessons of a philosophy course
Using it in casual conversation where metaphysics is the normal word

senses.definition: In a fluent manner, as expressing oneself easily, especially in a foreign language.
senses.example: He lived in Mexico, so he is able to speak Spanish fluently.

senses.definition: In a fluent manner, as having graceful movements.
In a fluent manner, as literally flowing.

core.definition: In a smooth, easy way, especially when speaking or writing a language without hesitation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The 'nt' cluster is often shortened; say 'FLOO-uhnt-lee' with a clear t and a soft 'lee' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises ease and skill.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fluently mostly with verbs like speak, read, write, or understand, as in 'She speaks Korean fluently.' It is used in everyday speech and in professional settings. Avoid using it for physical movement; graceful movement is better described as 'smoothly' or 'gracefully'.

distinctions.note: Well is general, while fluently emphasizes smooth, natural flow with few pauses.
Accurately concerns correctness; fluently concerns ease and smoothness.

examples.everyday: My daughter's friend speaks Arabic fluently, so she translated the menu for us at the restaurant.
examples.professional: Our new hire writes fluently in English and German, which helps with our European documentation.
examples.analytical: The author writes fluently, but her argument depends on a rhetorical flow that hides some logical gaps.

nuance.analogy: Speaking fluently is like a river running over smooth stones, without pausing or splashing.
nuance.etymology: From fluent (from Latin fluens, 'flowing') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing 'fluently' before the main verb in long sentences, where it sounds awkward.
Using 'fluently' for someone who only knows basic phrases.

senses.definition: A prediction of the weather.
senses.example: The forecast said it'll be blowy tomorrow

senses.definition: An estimation of a future condition.
senses.example: The forecast said it'll be blowy tomorrow

senses.definition: Exacta.
To estimate how something will be in the future.
senses.example: to forecast the weather, or a storm

senses.definition: To foreshadow; to suggest something in advance.

core.definition: A prediction of what the weather or another future condition will be, based on available information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -cast rhymes with 'past', not with 'vast' or 'cast' in the British sense. Pronounce the r after the vowel, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a forecast is simply an estimate, though it can be wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forecast constantly for the weather, as in 'What's the forecast for tomorrow?' It is also common at work for sales, budgets and project timelines. The verb is often used in the past tense as either forecast or forecasted, and both are accepted in American business writing. In casual talk, people often say 'the weather says' rather than forecast.

distinctions.note: Prediction is the general word for any statement about the future; forecast is more often used for weather, data or business estimates.
A projection is an estimate based on specific assumptions, often shown as numbers or a model; a forecast is usually the final estimate that people use.

examples.everyday: The weather forecast says it's going to rain all weekend, so we should move the picnic.
examples.professional: I need the revised revenue forecast by Thursday so we can update the budget before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: Keynes argues that any economic forecast depends on assumptions about human expectations, which makes precise prediction uncertain.

nuance.analogy: Like a navigator's estimate of where the ship will be by nightfall, based on speed, wind and course.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English forecast, from fore, before, and cast, to calculate or throw.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'cast' with a short a in the British way; American English usually uses the 'cast' sound with a short a, but the stress is the key point.
Using forecast as a noun for a single event rather than an estimate of future conditions.

conversation.text: What's the forecast for the weekend?
The forecast says sunny and eighty.
They're forecasting a big snowstorm on Tuesday.

senses.definition: The action of forgiving.
senses.example: He begged for forgiveness after being caught stealing from the shop.

senses.definition: A readiness to forgive.

core.definition: The act of pardoning someone for a wrong and letting go of anger or the wish for punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: fur-GIV-nus. The first syllable has an r-colored schwa, and the ending is a reduced 'nus', not 'ness' said clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests mercy, generosity, and healing, though it can feel difficult or costly in personal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'forgiveness' in personal, religious, and legal settings. Typical phrases are 'ask for forgiveness' and 'seek forgiveness'. A well-known saying is 'It's easier to ask forgiveness than permission,' which treats it humorously. In casual apologies, people say 'Forgive me' or 'I'm sorry' rather than 'I beg your forgiveness,' which sounds formal or dated.

distinctions.note: Pardon is often official or legal, like a governor's pardon; forgiveness is personal and emotional.
Mercy is compassion shown by someone with power to punish; forgiveness is releasing the debt or resentment.
Forgiveness can be one-sided, while reconciliation restores the relationship and needs both parties.

examples.everyday: I called my brother to ask for his forgiveness after what I said at dinner.
examples.professional: Our team culture values learning from mistakes, with forgiveness rather than blame as the default response.
examples.analytical: Many theologians distinguish forgiveness, a unilateral act of release, from reconciliation, which requires repentance and restored trust.

nuance.analogy: Like canceling a debt: you decide not to collect what you are owed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English forgiefnes, from forgiefan, 'to give up, grant, pardon.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a full 'ness' instead of 'nus'.
Using 'forgive to someone' instead of 'forgive someone'.
Saying 'ask forgiveness to' rather than 'ask someone's forgiveness' or 'ask for forgiveness'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew salach ('to pardon') and Greek aphesis ('release, forgiveness') carry the sense of sending away a debt or offense. Psalm 103:12 says God removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. Matthew 6:12-15 links asking God's forgiveness with forgiving others. Ephesians 1:7 says we have redemption and forgiveness through Christ's blood.

forgiveness.etymology: From Middle English *forgiveness,forgifnes*, from Old English *forġiefnes*.

senses.definition: A method of biblical criticism that classifies units of scripture by literary pattern and then attempts to trace each type to its period of oral transmission.

core.definition: A method of biblical study that sorts texts into literary types and traces each type back to its oral origins before it was written down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KRIT, the second word's first syllable. Keep the rhotic r in form, and reduce the unstressed vowels in 'criticism' so it sounds like 'KRIT-ih-siz-um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an academic term used in biblical scholarship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use form criticism mainly in seminaries, university religion departments, and scholarly writing about the Bible. In church conversations, people might say 'historical-critical approaches' instead. The term comes from German scholarship, and it is often discussed alongside source and redaction criticism.

distinctions.note: Source criticism identifies written documents behind a text; form criticism focuses on oral forms and their settings.
Redaction criticism studies how an editor shaped the final text; form criticism studies the smaller units and their earlier life.
Textual criticism compares manuscripts to reconstruct the original wording; form criticism analyzes literary genre and oral history.

antonyms: literary criticism of the final text

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader said the Psalms are easier to understand once you know a little form criticism.
examples.professional: In the seminar, we used form criticism to compare the lament psalms with similar community prayers from the ancient Near East.
examples.analytical: Form criticism assumes that the genre of a unit shaped its transmission, so a psalm of lament is read in relation to the setting in which it was spoken.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting old family recipes into categories before tracing which ones were passed down by word of mouth.
nuance.etymology: From German Formgeschichte, the method developed by Hermann Gunkel and others in the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using form criticism to mean any analysis of the form of a text, rather than the specific method of oral genre study.
Confusing it with form, the general word for a document's structure.
nuance.biblical_note: Form criticism was developed mainly for the Psalms, Genesis, and the Gospels. Hermann Gunkel classified psalms into types such as hymns, individual laments, and thanksgiving songs. He treated Psalm 13 as an individual lament, which helps show how form critics link a text's genre to its life setting in worship or community speech.

senses.definition: A person who flees from law enforcement, typically to avoid being arrested, prosecuted, or imprisoned.
A person who flees to escape persecution, danger (war, etc), or any unwanted situation.
Something fleeting; something hard to catch and detain.
Fleeing or running away; escaping.
Transient, fleeting or ephemeral.
Elusive or difficult to retain.
To render someone a fugitive; to drive into escape or exile.

core.definition: A person who runs away from the law, typically to avoid arrest, prosecution, or imprisonment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FYOO. Say the middle as 'juh' with a reduced vowel, and end with a short 'iv'. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies someone evading justice, though it can be sympathetic when used of people fleeing persecution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fugitive' mainly in news, legal, and police contexts, as in 'an escaped fugitive' or 'a federal fugitive'. Everyday speakers often say 'on the run' or 'wanted'. The word also has a broader sense for someone fleeing danger, but it is most closely tied to crime.

distinctions.note: A refugee flees a country because of war, persecution, or disaster, while a fugitive is usually running from law enforcement.
An escapee has broken out of prison or custody; a fugitive may be on the run from a crime without ever being jailed.
Criminal describes anyone who has committed a crime, but a fugitive is specifically a person evading capture.

examples.everyday: Did you see the news about the fugitive who escaped from the county jail?
examples.professional: Our security team is tracking a fugitive who may have used a stolen company badge to leave the building.
examples.analytical: The gospel narrative presents the sinner as a fugitive from divine justice, seeking a refuge in God's mercy.

nuance.analogy: A fugitive is like a shadow trying to stay out of the light of the law.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fugitivus, from fugere, meaning 'to flee'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable as 'fyoo-jih-TEEV'.
Using 'fugitive' for a refugee fleeing a country, which sounds accusatory and mismatches the situation.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the idea of the fugitive for people who flee from God's judgment or from violence. Cain, after killing Abel, is told he will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, which the Hebrew word nad (wanderer) reinforces. Moses flees from Pharaoh into Midian after killing an Egyptian, and Hagar flees from Sarai into the wilderness.

fugitive.etymology: From Middle English *fugitive*, *fugityve*, *fugityf*, *fugitife*, *fugytif*, *fugitif*, from Latin *fugitīvus*, from *fugitō*, from *fugiō*.

senses.definition: Huge; immense; tremendous.

core.definition: Extremely large, huge, or enormous, often used for tasks, portions, or problems.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, GAN. Say the ch-u part as one sound, like 'choo,' and keep the last syllable light, so it's not 'gar-GAN-too-ahn.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. It usually describes something overwhelming or excessive, and can be humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gargantuan in conversation, writing, and news to describe a big task, a huge serving, or a massive expense, often with a light, slightly exaggerated tone. In casual talk, huge or enormous is more common, so gargantuan can sound a little dramatic. It is comfortable in professional writing when describing scale.

distinctions.note: Huge is everyday and neutral; gargantuan is stronger and more dramatic, suggesting something nearly overwhelming.
Immense stresses vast size or extent, often in a neutral or admiring way, while gargantuan often carries a sense of excess or burden.

examples.everyday: That burrito was gargantuan; I could only eat half of it.
examples.professional: Migrating the legacy database is a gargantuan task, so we should break it into smaller phases.
examples.analytical: The gargantuan scale of modern data sets challenges older assumptions about what a model can reasonably learn.

nuance.analogy: Like a giant sandwich that takes a whole table to hold, far beyond what one person can finish.
nuance.etymology: From Gargantua, the giant in François Rabelais's 16th-century satirical novel.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle sound as 'gar-gan-TOO-ahn' with the stress shifted.
Using gargantuan for ordinary size; it is strong, so save it for truly large things.

gargantuan.etymology: From French *Gargantua*, a giant with a very large appetite in Rabelais's The Inestimable Life of Gargantua.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name in the Old Testament, borne by two men in the time of Jeremiah: a son of Shaphan and a son of Hilkiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the 'RY' syllable. The final syllable is an unstressed 'uh', not a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in Bible study, scholarly discussion of Jeremiah and Hebrew names. Ordinary conversation would not use it.

distinctions.note: Gedaliah is a different Hebrew name, borne by a governor of Judah; Gemariah is the name of Jeremiah-era scribes or officials.

examples.everyday: I noticed in the Jeremiah reading that Gemariah is a name that appears twice, so I asked which one was which.
examples.professional: In the study notes, Gemariah son of Shaphan is identified as one of the officials who heard Baruch read the scroll.
examples.analytical: The double appearance of the name Gemariah in Jeremiah raises questions about the identity of the court officials involved.

nuance.analogy: Like two people in a city with the same common name, where the context tells you which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew, meaning roughly 'Yahweh has accomplished' or 'Yahweh has completed'; the exact sense is debated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'GEM-uh-ry-uh'.
Confusing Gemariah with Gedaliah, a different name.
nuance.biblical_note: Gemariah son of Shaphan appears in Jeremiah 36:10-12, where he hears Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll in the chamber of the scribe and pleads with the officials not to let the king burn it. Gemariah son of Hilkiah appears in Jeremiah 29:3, where he carries a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon. The two men are distinguished by their fathers' names.

senses.definition: The use of templates, etc. to create generic source code that can be used in many situations.

core.definition: Programming features that let one piece of code work with many data types, written once with type placeholders.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NEH. The -ics ending is unstressed and sounds like 'iks,' not 'ee-ks.' Many learners add an extra syllable here.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American software teams, 'generics' is usually said in the plural and often with the language name, as in 'Java generics.' It is a technical term, so use it in code reviews, design discussions, and documentation. In C++ the usual term is 'templates,' so say 'templates' when talking about C++.

distinctions.note: 'Templates' is the C++ term for the same idea. 'Generics' is the common term in Java, C#, Kotlin, and TypeScript.
Polymorphism is the broader idea that one interface can have many forms. Generics is one specific way to achieve it through type parameters.

examples.everyday: My friend who codes in Java says the new library relies heavily on generics, so she had to learn it fast.
examples.professional: We should add generics to the cache class so it can store any object type without casting.
examples.analytical: Generics shift the type-checking burden from runtime to compile time, which narrows the class of bugs a program can contain.

nuance.analogy: Like a shipping container designed to hold any kind of cargo: the box stays the same, and only the contents change.
nuance.etymology: Plural of 'generic,' from Latin 'genus' (kind, class).
common_mistakes: Saying 'generic' for the whole concept: the usual plural noun is 'generics' or 'generic types.'
Mispronouncing the stress as 'JEN-er-iks.'

senses.definition: Of or relating to geopolitics.

core.definition: Relating to geopolitics: how geography, resources and power shape relations between countries and regions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIT, the third syllable. 'Geo' is pronounced JEE-oh, and the ending reduces to 'ih-kul', not 'ee-cal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes analysis of power and territory, sometimes implying great-power rivalry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it often in news and foreign policy talk, as in 'geopolitical tensions' or 'geopolitical risk.' It sounds analytical, so in casual conversation people more often say 'what's going on in the world' or 'world politics.' The noun for the field is geopolitics.

distinctions.note: Political is general about government and power; geopolitical adds the role of geography, territory and resources.
International describes relations between nations generally; geopolitical stresses strategic power competition and location.
Global refers to worldwide scope or reach; geopolitical refers to power among states.

examples.everyday: Gas prices jumped again, and everybody blames some geopolitical mess overseas.
examples.professional: Our supply chain team flagged geopolitical risk in two key suppliers, so we're diversifying our sourcing.
examples.analytical: Any account of the Cold War must treat ideology and geopolitical interest as intertwined rather than as separate causes.

nuance.analogy: Politics is the game; geopolitics is the board's shape, with its rivers, mountains and borders deciding which moves are possible.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ge, 'earth,' plus political.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as geo-PO-li-tical; the main stress is on LIT.
Using 'geopolitical' as a noun; the field is 'geopolitics' and the adjective is 'geopolitical'.
Using it for any political issue; the word specifically concerns geography and power.

senses.definition: To return to a place or state after having been there at a previous time.
senses.example: We were getting cold so we decided to go back.

core.definition: To return to a place, a previous state, a topic, or a point in time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'back', and the vowel is the short a as in 'cat'. In casual speech, 'go back' sounds like 'guh-BAK' with a quick link.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it describes movement or return, with no emotional charge unless context adds it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go back' for physical return, such as 'I need to go back to the office', and also for returning to a topic: 'Let's go back to the budget question.' It can also mean a history: 'This tradition goes back to 1850.' The phrase is informal enough for everyday talk and common in business meetings.

distinctions.note: 'Return' is more formal and often used in writing or for objects, while 'go back' is common in speech and applies to places, topics, and time.
'Come back' is used from the speaker's or listener's perspective, while 'go back' is used when the movement is away from the speaker's current place.

examples.everyday: I forgot my keys, so I have to go back to the apartment.
examples.professional: Before we finalize the report, let's go back to the data and check the outliers.
examples.analytical: To understand the doctrine, we must go back to its earliest textual sources.

nuance.analogy: It is like rewinding a video to a earlier scene and playing it again from there.
common_mistakes: Saying 'go back to home' instead of 'go back home', since 'home' works as an adverb here.
Confusing 'go back' with 'come back' when the speaker is in the destination.
Forgetting that 'go back on' is a different phrase meaning to break a promise.

conversation.text: I have to go back home, I forgot my wallet.
We went back to that Italian place we loved.
Mark and I go back a long way; we were in college together.

senses.definition: To discontinue engaging in criminal acts; to become a law-abiding person.

core.definition: To stop committing crimes and start living as a law-abiding person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STRAIGHT, and the word is pronounced with a single syllable, so the gh is silent. The t is a clear t, not a flap, because it begins a stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing reform, but it can be a little judgmental if said about someone who is still suspected of crime.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go straight' most often in conversations or stories about a former criminal, such as 'He did three years, and he's trying to go straight now.' It is informal and usually used in past or ongoing narrative. It should not be confused with the directions sense, which is about travel. A natural reply is 'I hope he does, he deserves a second chance.'

distinctions.note: Go legit is more informal slang that means to start legal business after illegal activity, while go straight is the more general term for leaving crime.
Reform is a formal word for improving behavior or institutions, while go straight is a casual, personal expression about leaving crime.

examples.everyday: My cousin got out of prison last year and says he really wants to go straight now.
examples.professional: Our reentry program helps people who want to go straight find stable jobs and housing.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether a person who wants to go straight can escape the stigma of a past conviction.

nuance.analogy: Like a road that bends away from trouble and runs in one clear direction.
common_mistakes: Confusing the crime sense with the travel sense: 'go straight' in directions means keep moving ahead, not stop crime.
Adding 'to' before a noun, as in 'go straight to the police'; the meaning there is direction, not reform.

conversation.text: Go straight through the next light.
Go straight for a mile, and you'll see the hospital.
Don't turn yet; go straight until you hit Main Street.

senses.definition: Meet someone for a casual drink, often after work.

core.definition: To meet someone for a casual drink, often after work.

pronunciation.tip: Link the words smoothly as grab-uh-DRINK. The a is a quick uh sound, and the stress falls on drink.

nuance.connotation: Positive; casual, social, and friendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for relaxed social meetups, often after work or on a weekend, where the drink may be beer, wine, or a cocktail. Coffee is grab coffee instead. A natural reply is Sure, where? or Sounds fun. Alcohol is common but not required, since soda or tea can also work.

distinctions.note: Grab a drink often implies alcohol; grab coffee specifically means a coffee meeting.
Have a drink does not suggest arranging a meeting; grab a drink usually means meeting up on purpose.

examples.everyday: Hey, want to grab a drink after the game on Saturday?
examples.professional: A few of us are going to grab a drink after the offsite; you're welcome to join.
examples.analytical: The sociologist notes that many professional relationships begin when colleagues grab a drink after work rather than in formal meetings.

nuance.analogy: It's a short, casual stop in a busy day, like a friendly hello in the hallway with a glass in hand.
common_mistakes: Using grab a drink for a formal business meeting; say meet or get together instead.
Assuming it always means alcohol; the phrase can also mean a soda or tea.

conversation.text: A few of us are going to grab a drink after work. You in?
We should grab a drink sometime. I'd love to hear about the new job.
"Want to grab a drink?" "Sure, there's a nice bar around the corner."

senses.definition: A small shoot or scion of a tree inserted in another tree, the stock of which is to support and nourish it. The two unite and become one tree, but the graft determines the kind of fruit.
A branch or portion of a tree growing from such a shoot.
A portion of living tissue used in the operation of autoplasty.
The depth of the blade of a digging tool such as a spade or shovel.
A narrow spade used in digging drainage trenches.
Corruption in official life.
Illicit profit by corrupt means, especially in public life.
A criminal’s special branch of practice.
A con job.
A cut of the take (money).
A bribe, especially on an ongoing basis.
To insert (a graft) in a branch or stem of another tree; to propagate by insertion in another stock; also, to insert a graft upon.
To insert scions (grafts) from one tree, or kind of tree, etc. into another; to practice grafting.
To implant a portion of (living flesh or akin) in a lesion so as to form an organic union.
To join (one thing) to another as if by grafting, so as to bring about a close union.
To work hard.
To obtain illegal gain from bribery or similar corrupt practices.
To cover, as a ring bolt, block strap, splicing, etc. with a weaving of small cord or rope yarns.
To form a graft polymer.

core.definition: Money or advantage gained dishonestly by someone using a public position, especially in politics or government contracts.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with 'raft' and 'craft', with a short a and a sharp t at the end. Do not add a vowel after g, and do not say 'graf-t'.

nuance.connotation: negative. It describes corruption and dishonesty in public life.
nuance.usage_note: In American news and political conversation, 'graft' usually means corrupt political profit, as in 'city hall graft'. In medicine and gardening, it means a transplanted tissue or a shoot joined to a plant, and context makes the meaning clear. Americans may also say 'corruption' or 'kickbacks' for similar meanings.

distinctions.note: Corruption is the broader term for dishonest misuse of power, while graft usually refers to the money or favors gained through it.
A kickback is a secret payment for a favor, which is one specific form of graft.

examples.everyday: People in town are angry because the mayor's brother got the road contract, and they're calling it graft.
examples.professional: The internal audit flagged graft in the procurement process, so the contract was frozen until the review ends.
examples.analytical: Graft erodes public trust because it converts public office into private gain, and it undermines the legitimacy of the institutions that govern.

nuance.analogy: Graft is like a tap that drains the public water tank into private buckets.
nuance.etymology: From Old French greffe, from Latin graphium, stylus, from Greek graphein, to write, a sense that came to mean grafting a shoot onto a plant.
common_mistakes: Using graft only for tree grafting and missing its political meaning.
Mispronouncing it as 'graf' or 'graft' with an extra vowel.

graft.etymology: From Middle English *graffe*, from Old French *greffe* (“stylus”), from Latin *graphium* (“stylus”), from Ancient Greek *γραφείον*, from *γράφειν* (“to write”); probably akin to.

senses.definition: A condition of total, interlocking traffic congestion on the streets or highways of a crowded city, in which no one can move because everyone is in someone else's way.

On a smaller scale, the situation in which cars enter a signal-controlled intersection too late during the green light cycle, and are unable to clear the intersection (due to congestion in the next block) when the light turns red, thus blocking the cross traffic when it's their turn to go. Repeated at enough intersections, this phenomenon can lead to citywide gridlock.
Any paralysis of a complex system due to severe congestion, conflict, or deadlock.
Deliberate misspelling of girlcock and girldick.
To cause traffic congestion.

core.definition: Traffic so jammed that no vehicle can move, because each car blocks the others in a crowded city or on a highway.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GRID most strongly, with a weaker secondary stress on lock. In General American the vowel in lock matches cot, so say it as LAHK, not LOK.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a frustrating situation where nothing moves.
nuance.usage_note: Gridlock is common American English for severe traffic jams, used often in traffic reports and by commuters. It is also used figuratively for political or institutional deadlock, as in Congress is in gridlock. For casual talk you can say we're stuck in traffic, but gridlock is natural for a bad jam.

distinctions.note: Traffic jam is the general everyday term; gridlock stresses that nothing can move at all, often across many blocks.
Deadlock is the general term for a stalemate, while gridlock is typically used for traffic or government stalemates.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, there was gridlock on the interstate.
examples.professional: Our release is stuck in gridlock because two teams are waiting on each other's approval.
examples.analytical: Under such conditions, each agent's rational choice produces collective gridlock, a failure that no single actor can resolve.

nuance.analogy: Like a drain where every bit of water is stuck behind the next, gridlock stops the whole flow.
nuance.etymology: From grid, a network of crossing lines, plus lock, to fasten together, from the image of interlocked traffic.
common_mistakes: Using gridlock for any slow traffic; a slow commute is not gridlock unless almost nothing moves.
Stressing the second word, grid-LOCK, instead of GRID-lock.

conversation.text: Downtown was total gridlock after the concert ended.
A water main break caused gridlock across the whole city.
There's so much gridlock in Congress that nothing gets passed.

senses.definition: The worship of saints.

core.definition: Excessive veneration or worship of saints; a term often used critically by those who think such devotion goes too far.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, AH. The middle -o- reduces to 'uh', and the g is hard. Do not say 'hag-ee-OL-a-try' with a long o.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative or polemical, implying that honor given to saints has become worship; Catholics and Orthodox reject the label.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, specialized word found in theology and church history. It is mostly used by critics, especially in Protestant polemic. Many Christians would say they venerate, not worship, saints.

distinctions.note: Veneration is respect and honor that does not claim to be worship; hagiolatry claims or implies worship.
Idolatry is worship of any created thing; hagiolatry is specifically worship of saints.
Hagiography is writing about saints; hagiolatry is the devotion itself.

examples.everyday: My Protestant friend says praying to saints sounds like hagiolatry, but my Catholic neighbor disagrees.
examples.professional: In this seminar, we will examine how Reformation critics labeled certain cults of saints as hagiolatry.
examples.analytical: Whether the honor given to saints constitutes hagiolatry depends on the distinction between latria, due to God alone, and dulia, due to saints.

nuance.analogy: Hagiolatry is admiration of a saint that critics think has crossed the line into worship.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hagios, 'holy', plus latreia, 'worship'.
common_mistakes: Misplacing the stress on the first or last syllable.
Treating it as a neutral term; it is usually a charge.
Confusing it with 'hagiography'.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture commands worship of God alone (Exodus 20:3-5; Matthew 4:10). In Revelation 19:10 and 22:8-9, John is rebuked by an angel when he falls down to worship him. These passages are often cited in debates about the limits of honoring saints.

traditions.view: Saints are venerated, not worshiped; worship (latreia) belongs to God alone. Asking saints to pray for us is seen as the communion of the Church in Christ.
Catholics distinguish latria (worship, due to God alone) from dulia (veneration of saints), and hyperdulia for Mary. They reject the claim that this is hagiolatry.

Most Protestants reject invocation of saints as lacking biblical warrant and risking idolatry, though Lutherans and Anglicans honor saints as examples of faith. Some critics use hagiolatry as a charge against Catholic and Orthodox practice.

senses.definition: Any of several plant-eating mammals of the genus Lepus, similar to a rabbit, but larger and with longer ears.
The meat from this animal.
The player in a paperchase, or hare and hounds game, who leaves a trail of paper to be followed.
To move swiftly.
Gray, hoary; gray-haired, venerable (of people).
senses.example: a hare old man

senses.definition: Cold, frosty (of weather).
senses.example: a hare day

core.definition: A fast, long-eared mammal like a rabbit but larger, with longer legs and ears, that lives above ground in open fields.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable that sounds exactly like 'hair'. Keep the r sound, and do not add a y or an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The idiom 'mad as a March hare' suggests wild or frantic behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hare for larger, fast animals, and the western jackrabbit is a hare, while rabbit is the everyday word for most smaller animals. Hares are born with fur and open eyes, unlike baby rabbits. As a verb, hare means to run fast, as in 'he hared off down the street', which sounds literary. Hare and hair are homophones, so check spelling carefully.

distinctions.note: Hares are larger, with longer ears and legs, and live in open fields rather than in burrows, while rabbits usually live in burrows.
Jackrabbit is an American name for a hare, not a different animal, and it is common in the western United States.

examples.everyday: We saw a hare racing across the field near the trail this morning.
examples.professional: The wildlife survey counted hare sightings along each transect and compared them with rabbit numbers.
examples.analytical: The Levitical dietary law classes the hare as unclean, a judgment that treats its cud-chewing as incomplete without a divided hoof.

nuance.analogy: A hare is a rabbit that never went to ground: it stays in the open and relies on speed.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hara, related to German Hase.
common_mistakes: Confusing hare with hair, since they sound identical but have unrelated meanings.
Using hare for every small animal; Americans usually call small wild animals rabbits.
nuance.biblical_note: The hare appears in the dietary laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy as an unclean animal because it chews the cud but does not divide the hoof. The Hebrew word is arnebet. Leviticus 11:6 gives this reason, and Deuteronomy 14:7 repeats the prohibition in its list of animals not to be eaten. Christians generally read these laws as part of Israel's ceremonial law rather than as a binding food rule for believers today.

senses.definition: An inductive generalization based on insufficient evidence or data, leading to a rushed conclusion.

core.definition: A conclusion drawn from too few or unrepresentative examples, reached before the evidence can support it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -ZAY- in generalization, and the first word has a light secondary stress on HAY. Say 'JEN-er' with the r coloring the vowel, and avoid a stressed final -tion.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a logical error, so calling someone's argument a hasty generalization is a criticism.
nuance.usage_note: This is a standard term in logic, critical thinking, and academic writing, and Americans use it when pointing out flawed reasoning, often politely, as in 'That's a bit of a hasty generalization.' In casual conversation people would say 'you're jumping to conclusions' instead. A natural reply is 'Fair point, I need more data.'

distinctions.note: Jumping to conclusions is the everyday phrase for reaching a decision too quickly, while hasty generalization is the precise logical term for drawing a broad claim from too little evidence.
Sampling bias concerns a sample that is systematically unrepresentative, while hasty generalization concerns a sample that is simply too small or too narrow.

examples.everyday: You can't say all dogs bite just because one bit you; that's a hasty generalization.
examples.professional: Our churn analysis looked at only two regions, so concluding that customers in general are leaving would be a hasty generalization.
examples.analytical: To infer a universal claim from a handful of cases is a hasty generalization, which the inductive logician must guard against by enlarging the sample.

nuance.analogy: A hasty generalization is like tasting one grape from a bunch and declaring the whole vineyard sour.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hasty generalization' with British spelling in American writing.
Using it for any quick decision instead of a conclusion drawn from insufficient evidence.

senses.definition: A curve on the surface of a cylinder or cone such that its angle to a plane perpendicular to the axis is constant; the three-dimensional curve seen in a screw or a spiral staircase.
A small volute under the abacus of a Corinthian capital.
An upside down midair 360° spin in playboating.
The incurved rim of the external ear.
senses.example: helix piercing

senses.definition: To form or cause to form a helix.

core.definition: A curve that winds around a cylinder or cone at a constant angle, like the thread of a screw or a spiral staircase.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HEE, and make the last sound a crisp x-like 'ks'. Do not add an extra syllable as in heh-LEE-ex.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise geometric or biological term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use helix in math, biology, chemistry, and engineering, and also in everyday talk about DNA's double helix. In casual speech people often say 'spiral' or 'coil' instead, but 'double helix' is common in science news.

distinctions.note: A spiral can lie flat in a plane, such as a snail shell, while a helix is three-dimensional and climbs along an axis.
A coil is a general term for something wound, often in wire, while a helix has a precise geometric definition.

examples.everyday: The spring in this pen has a tight helix, so it snaps back every time.
examples.professional: We modeled the sensor cable as a helix so the bend radius stays within spec.
examples.analytical: Under the parametrization x equals cos t, y equals sin t, z equals ct, the curve is a helix with constant angle to the z-axis.

nuance.analogy: A helix is like the path of a screw thread: every turn climbs at the same steady height.
nuance.etymology: From Greek helix, 'spiral, coil', related to helissein, 'to turn round'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long I as HY-licks.
Confusing helix with helices, its plural, which is pronounced HEL-ih-seez.

helix.etymology: From Latin *helix*, from Ancient Greek *ἕλιξ* (“something twisted or spiral”).

senses.definition: The religious practices of the Hesychasts.

core.definition: The Eastern Orthodox tradition of contemplative prayer seeking inner stillness and union with God, especially through the Jesus Prayer and experience of divine light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the 'y' sounds like a short i and the 'ch' is a hard k. The ending -asm is 'az-um', like 'spasm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; reverent within Orthodoxy, though historically contested by critics like Barlaam.
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in theology, church history and discussions of Orthodox spirituality. An ordinary American would not know it. The practitioner is a Hesychast.

distinctions.note: Quietism is a passive-leaning doctrine often condemned in the West; Hesychasm is a disciplined ascetic practice of prayer.
Contemplation is a general term; Hesychasm names a specific Orthodox method and theology.
Mysticism is the broad category; Hesychasm is one Eastern Christian form of it.

examples.everyday: My friend from the Orthodox church told me Hesychasm is all about learning to pray in silence.
examples.professional: Today's lecture will trace Hesychasm from the Desert Fathers to Mount Athos in the fourteenth century.
examples.analytical: Gregory Palamas defended Hesychasm by distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies, which can be experienced.

nuance.analogy: Like tuning out all radio static until you can hear one clear station.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hesychia, 'stillness, quiet', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'ch' as in 'church' instead of /k/.
Stressing the second syllable: say HESS-ih-kaz-um.
Confusing it with general quietism.
nuance.biblical_note: The ideal draws on Greek hesychia, 'quietness'. In 1 Thessalonians 4:11 Paul urges believers to aim to live quietly. Matthew 6:6 speaks of praying in your inner room, which Hesychasts read as inward prayer. The transfiguration in Matthew 17:1-8 is taken as the model of seeing divine light.
