Using the verb for a party is informal, so say 'We're going to tailgate before the game' among friends.

distinctions.note: Following is neutral and describes any distance behind a car; tailgate implies the distance is unsafe or rude.
Cutting off means changing lanes in front of someone; tailgating means driving too close behind them.

examples.everyday: Hey, back off a little, you're tailgating me in this rain.
examples.professional: Our security team reported someone tailgating through the side door of the lab, so please badge in with your own card.
examples.analytical: To tailgate in traffic is to shrink the margin of safety, whereas in access control it means exploiting another person's legitimate entry.

nuance.analogy: Like a rider drafting so closely behind a racer that he gets pulled along without any effort of his own.
nuance.etymology: From tail plus gate; the gate is the hinged board at the back of a wagon or truck.
common_mistakes: Using tailgate only for a party; in traffic, the verb means driving too close.
Stressing the second syllable, saying tail-GATE, instead of TAIL-gate.

conversation.text: Don't tailgate; you can't stop in time if he brakes.
The truck behind me tailgated me for ten miles.
We tailgate before every home game with burgers in the parking lot.
Put the cooler on the tailgate.
We're going to tailgate before the game. Want to come?
The tailgate starts at ten in the stadium parking lot.
Stop tailgating that car; you're way too close.

senses.definition: To swim.

core.definition: To swim briefly, usually in a pool, lake or ocean, for a quick cool-down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DIP. Keep the short i in dip, and in fast speech take a sounds like tay-kuh.

nuance.connotation: Positive and relaxed. It suggests a refreshing swim on a warm day.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use take a dip for a short, casual swim, especially on vacation or in summer. For a longer swim, say 'go for a swim'. A natural reply is 'Sounds great, I'll grab the towels.'

distinctions.note: Go for a swim is the usual phrase for a longer, more deliberate swim; take a dip is shorter and more casual.
Take a plunge can mean jumping into water boldly, or a risky financial commitment; take a dip is only about swimming.

collocations: take a dip in the lake
take a dip in the pool

examples.everyday: It's ninety degrees, let's take a dip in the lake before dinner.
examples.professional: After the offsite, a few of us took a dip in the hotel pool before the team dinner.
examples.analytical: The phrase relies on a metaphor of immersion, where a brief dip signals a temporary and partial contact with an element.

nuance.analogy: Like touching a toe into a lake to test it, then deciding to fully jump in.
nuance.etymology: Take from Old Norse taka; dip from Old English dyppan.
common_mistakes: Using take a dip for a long swim, when go for a swim is more natural.
Confusing dip with deep, which changes both the sound and the meaning.

conversation.text: It's so hot; let's take a dip in the lake.
I'm going to take a quick dip before dinner.
Do you want to take a dip, or are you staying on the beach?

senses.definition: To leave the ground and ascend into the air or into flight.
senses.example: The plane has been cleared to take off from runway 3.

senses.definition: To become successful, to flourish.
senses.example: The business has really taken off this year and has made quite a profit.

senses.definition: To remove.
senses.example: He took off his shoes.

senses.definition: To take (a specified time period) as a vacation or break from work or other activity.
senses.example: I'd like to take next Friday off to attend a wedding.

senses.definition: To absent oneself from work or other responsibility, especially with permission.
senses.example: If you take off for Thanksgiving you must work Christmas and vice versa.

senses.definition: To depart.
senses.example: I'm going to take off now.

senses.definition: To stand up on a surfboard and begin to surf a breaking wave.
To imitate (somebody), often in a satirical manner.
senses.example: Much of his act involves taking off the Prime Minister and other politicians.

senses.definition: To quantify.
senses.example: I'll take off the concrete and steel for this construction project.

senses.definition: To take drugs; to inject drugs.
To steal (something) or rob (someone).

core.definition: To remove clothing or an object, or for a plane to leave the ground, or to leave quickly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OFF, with a vowel close to 'caught'. In phrases, 'take off' links to 'tay-KAWF'. The t in 'take' is light.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'take off' for removing shoes or jackets at home, for a plane leaving the runway, and for a business or product becoming popular. 'I'm taking off' means I'm leaving now, which is casual. In a restaurant, you can ask 'Can I take off the lid?'

distinctions.note: 'Remove' is more formal and general; 'take off' is conversational and often used for clothing.
'Leave' is neutral; 'take off' suggests suddenness or informality.

examples.everyday: Please take off your shoes when you come in, the floor was just cleaned.
examples.professional: Our startup really started to take off after the product launch in March.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that rational inquiry can take off from ordinary observation, rising like a plane from the runway of experience.

nuance.analogy: Like a plane lifting from the runway, a small effort can suddenly rise into success.
common_mistakes: Using 'take off' as a noun without a hyphen in formal writing; 'takeoff' is the standard noun.
Confusing 'take off' with 'take off of'; 'off of' is not standard.

conversation.text: Please take off your shoes before coming inside.
Our flight took off an hour late.
Her business really took off last year.
I'm going to take off now, see you tomorrow.
I'm taking Friday off to go fishing.
It's late, so I'm going to take off.
Take off your shoes at security.
Our flight takes off at six in the morning.

senses.definition: In a tedious or wearisome manner.

core.definition: In a way that is long, slow, and boring, so that it tires or annoys you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. Keep the middle syllables short and weak, and end with a light 'lee' rather than a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes how something is done, usually with a sense of wearying slowness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tediously mostly in writing or formal speech to describe a slow process, as in 'The repairs proceeded tediously.' In everyday speech people more often say 'it took forever' or 'it was a slog.' It is rarely used to mean 'tiresomely rude' about a person.

distinctions.note: Slowly only describes speed; tediously adds that the slowness is boring or wearying.
Laboriously stresses great effort and hard work, while tediously stresses dullness and repetition.

examples.everyday: The line at the post office moved tediously, so I almost gave up.
examples.professional: The migration script ran tediously because it processed each record one at a time.
examples.analytical: The author tediously repeats the same distinction across three chapters without advancing the argument.

nuance.analogy: Tediously is like a slow song played at half speed: you can follow it, but every note drags.
nuance.etymology: Formed from tedious with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'tediously' to describe a person's character rather than a process.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural to American ears.

core.definition: A town in the hills of Judah, about ten miles south of Bethlehem, known as the home of the prophet Amos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'KOH'. Finish with a soft 'uh' rather than a hard 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name used in biblical and historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Tekoa mainly in Bible study, sermons, or history talks. Pronounce the place name the same way in conversation, and say 'the town of Tekoa' if you need to clarify. It is not a common word in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Tekoa refers to the town, while Tekoite refers to a person from it, such as Amos.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study read about Amos, and someone asked where Tekoa is.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, I placed Tekoa in Judah to show that the prophet spoke from outside the northern kingdom.
examples.analytical: Amos's self-description as a herdsman of Tekoa, in 1:1, shapes how readers understand his prophetic authority.

nuance.analogy: Tekoa is like a hometown mentioned in a story: it tells you where the speaker came from and why his voice carries an outsider's edge.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew tĕqoaʿ, a place name in Judah.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in TEK-oh-uh.
Pronouncing the final vowel as a hard 'ah' rather than a soft 'uh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Tekoa (Hebrew tĕqoaʿ) was a town in the hill country of Judah, about ten miles south of Jerusalem's neighbor Bethlehem, known for its shepherds and its wilderness. It is the hometown of the prophet Amos, who calls himself a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs (Amos 7:14). In 2 Samuel 14:2 Joab sends a wise woman from Tekoa to speak to King David, and in 2 Chronicles 11:6 King Rehoboam fortifies Tekoa among the cities of Judah. Jeremiah 6:1 also calls for a trumpet to be blown in Tekoa, a sign of warning.

senses.definition: Frightening or intimidating.
senses.example: terrifying creature

senses.definition: Of a formidable nature; terrific.

core.definition: Extremely frightening or intimidating, causing great fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Say the middle as 'rih' and the final '-ing' as a short, unstressed syllable, not 'eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something causing intense fear, and it is also used jokingly for something very difficult ('a terrifying exam').
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'terrifying' for frightening events, experiences, or people, such as 'a terrifying ride.' In casual speech it is often used with some exaggeration, as when someone says a phone bill is terrifying. Be careful with the older sense 'terrific' (wonderful), which is not used in modern American English. A natural reply is 'That sounds terrifying! Are you okay?'

distinctions.note: 'Scary' is casual and common, often for movies or Halloween. 'Terrifying' is stronger and can describe real danger.
'Frightening' is neutral and widely used. 'Terrifying' suggests a more extreme level of fear.

examples.everyday: That roller coaster was terrifying, but I loved it.
examples.professional: The prospect of a production database failure is terrifying, so we test our backups every month.
examples.analytical: The problem of evil is terrifying to many believers because it seems to challenge God's goodness.

nuance.analogy: A terrifying thing is like a dark hallway with a sudden loud noise: it makes you freeze.
nuance.etymology: From terrify, from Latin terrificare, to frighten.
common_mistakes: Using 'terrifying' to mean 'wonderful' as in old-fashioned 'terrific.'
Saying 'I am terrifying' instead of 'I am terrified' when describing your own feeling.

senses.definition: Saying the air conditioning is broken.

core.definition: A common sentence used to report that the air conditioning system is broken or not cooling the room.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters A and C separately as 'ay-see', with 'isn't' reduced quickly. The stress lands on WORK, and the r in working is American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical complaint or report.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when reporting a problem to a landlord, front desk, building manager or family member. In hot weather, people often say 'The AC is out' or 'The AC is broken' as well. Polite follow-ups include 'Could someone come take a look?' or 'When can someone check it?'

distinctions.note: Neutral and common; 'The AC is out' is more informal and casual.
More formal and complete; it suits written complaints or formal reports.

collocations: the AC is blowing warm air
call the landlord about the AC

examples.everyday: Hi, the AC isn't working in my apartment, and it's really hot in here.
examples.professional: Hi, I'm calling to report that the AC isn't working in Conference Room B, so the meeting may need to move.
examples.analytical: When the AC isn't working, the building's temperature control fails, which affects both comfort and equipment performance.

nuance.analogy: Like a fridge that stops humming: everything still exists, but the cooling is simply gone.
common_mistakes: Saying 'The AC is not work' without the -ing form.
Pronouncing 'AC' as a single word like 'ack' instead of 'ay-see'.

conversation.text: Hi, the AC isn't working, and it's ninety degrees in here.
The AC isn't working in the bedroom, so we slept in the living room.

core.definition: A clear sign of an approaching failure, defeat or unwelcome ending that people should recognize.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RY in writing and on WAWL, with ahn and thuh weak. Link the words so it sounds like 'thuh-RY-ting-ahn-thuh-WAWL'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns of trouble or the end of something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a situation clearly signals trouble, such as falling sales or repeated warnings from a manager. It is common in news and business talk, and it sounds dramatic, so use it carefully in formal settings. A natural reply is 'Yeah, we should have seen the writing on the wall.'

distinctions.note: A red flag is a warning sign that something needs attention. The writing on the wall suggests a definite, nearly inevitable outcome.
The handwriting on the wall is a variant with the same meaning. The writing on the wall is more common in American speech.

collocations: see the writing on the wall
the writing was on the wall
the writing on the wall for the company
read the writing on the wall

examples.everyday: When the factory closed its last shift, everyone in town could see the writing on the wall.
examples.professional: Three quarters of declining revenue is the writing on the wall, so we need a new plan before the board meets.
examples.analytical: Interpreting the writing on the wall requires separating visible signs from the deeper structural causes that produce them.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather radar that shows a storm coming before the first drop of rain.
nuance.etymology: From the biblical account in Daniel 5, in which writing appears on a wall at Belshazzar's feast.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the writing in the wall'; the preposition is on.
Using it for a neutral message; it signals a warning about a bad outcome.
nuance.biblical_note: In Daniel 5, King Belshazzar of Babylon holds a feast and sees a hand writing on the plaster of the palace wall. No one can read the writing until Daniel is brought in to interpret it. The Aramaic words are mene, mene, tekel and peres, which Daniel explains as a judgment that the king's reign is numbered, weighed and divided. Daniel 5:5 describes the appearance of the fingers writing. Daniel 5:25-28 gives Daniel's interpretation of the words. Belshazzar is killed that same night, according to Daniel 5:30.

senses.definition: A thing as it is independent of any conceptualization or perception by the human mind, postulated by practical reason but existing in a condition which is in principle unknowable and unexperienceable.

core.definition: In Kant's philosophy, a thing as it is in itself, independent of how the human mind perceives or conceptualizes it, and therefore unknowable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "self," the last syllable of the final word, while "thing" and "in" carry lighter secondary stress. Say "it" quickly and reduce it to "ut" in fast speech. The "ng" in "thing" is one sound, not "ng" plus "g."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in philosophy and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "thing-in-itself" mainly in philosophy courses, academic writing, and discussions of Kant. It usually appears in its German form, "Ding an sich," in scholarly texts. In everyday speech it would sound odd, so people use "reality" or "the thing as it really is."

distinctions.note: A phenomenon is a thing as it appears to us, while the thing-in-itself is the thing as it is independent of appearance.
Noumenon is a closely related Kantian term for an object of pure understanding; for Kant, the thing-in-itself is the unknowable reality behind appearances.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor said Kant believed we never know things exactly as they really are, which he called the thing-in-itself.
examples.professional: The essay argues that the thing-in-itself is useful as a limit concept even if it is not directly knowable.
examples.analytical: Kant's postulation of the thing-in-itself grounds his claim that appearances are structured by the mind without being created by it.

nuance.analogy: The thing-in-itself is like the actual fruit inside a sealed jar: you see its shape through the glass, but you never touch it directly.
nuance.etymology: A translation of German Ding an sich, the term used by Immanuel Kant in the 1780s.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphens and writing "thing in itself" in formal writing.
Confusing the thing-in-itself with the phenomenon, which is what appears to us.
Stressing "thing" as the main beat instead of "self."

senses.definition: Demonstrating thought or careful consideration.
senses.example: Most thoughtful people eventually solve the puzzle.

senses.definition: Demonstrating kindness or consideration for others.
senses.example: Preparing dinner is a thoughtful gesture for a new mother.

core.definition: Showing careful thought, or showing kindness and consideration for other people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ful is a reduced syllable pronounced 'fuhl', not 'fool'. Many Americans with the cot-caught merger say this with an 'ah' vowel, which is also acceptable.

nuance.connotation: positive; praising someone's care or consideration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'That's thoughtful of you' when someone gives a gift or does a kind favor. It can also describe a careful, reflective answer or essay. It is friendly and polite in everyday speech and common at work.

distinctions.note: Considerate focuses on avoiding harm or inconvenience to others, while thoughtful can also describe careful reflection.
Pensive describes a quiet, dreamy or sad mood, while thoughtful describes deliberate consideration.

examples.everyday: Thanks for bringing soup when I was sick, that was really thoughtful of you.
examples.professional: Thanks for the thoughtful feedback on the proposal, it helped us tighten the timeline.
examples.analytical: A thoughtful reading of the argument considers both its premises and the objections it anticipates.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-tuned instrument: each note is chosen with care so the whole piece sounds right.
nuance.etymology: From thought plus the suffix -ful, meaning full of thought.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'thought-FULL'.
Using thoughtful to mean thinking in general without the sense of care or consideration.

senses.definition: The characteristic of using a minimum of something (especially money).
senses.example: His thrift can be seen in how little the trashman takes from his house.

senses.definition: A savings bank.
senses.example: Usually, home mortgages are obtained from thrifts.

senses.definition: Any of various plants of the genus Armeria, particularly Armeria maritima.
To shop or browse at a thrift shop; to buy (something) at a thrift shop.
senses.example: They like to go thrifting on weekends.

core.definition: The habit of using money and resources carefully and avoiding waste; economical management.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin', and the vowel is short, as in 'sit'. Keep the final 'ft' as a clean consonant cluster, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive; thrift suggests responsible, admirable care with money, though it can slip toward stinginess when overdone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thrift to praise careful spending, especially in personal finance, family life, and shopping. In everyday talk, people more often say 'being frugal' or 'saving money', and thrift sounds slightly formal or traditional. The word also names a plant, Armeria maritima, but that sense is rare in daily speech.

distinctions.note: Frugality is a more deliberate and disciplined form of saving, while thrift is more about wise management of resources.
Economy can mean an economic system or efficiency, while thrift is personal care with money or resources.
Stinginess is negative and suggests refusing to spend even when it is reasonable; thrift is positive.

examples.everyday: My mom taught us the value of thrift, so we always fixed things instead of throwing them away.
examples.professional: Our procurement policy encourages thrift by requiring two quotes before any purchase over five hundred dollars.
examples.analytical: Early American writers often praised thrift as a Christian virtue, linking careful stewardship of money with moral discipline.

nuance.analogy: Thrift is like a gardener who uses every bit of rain and compost, so nothing goes to waste and the whole garden grows.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse þrift 'prosperity, success', from þrífa 'to grasp, thrive'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'th' as a voiced sound, as in 'this'.
Using thrift as an adjective; the adjective is thrifty.

thrift.etymology: From Middle English *thrift*, *thryfte*, *þrift*, from Old Norse *þrift* (“thriving condition, prosperity”).

senses.definition: An attack made by moving the sword parallel to its length and landing with the point.
senses.example: Pierre was a master swordsman, and could parry the thrusts of lesser men with barely a thought.

senses.definition: A push, stab, or lunge forward.
senses.example: The cutpurse tried to knock her satchel from her hands, but she avoided his thrust and yelled, "Thief!"

senses.definition: The force generated by propulsion, as in a jet engine.
senses.example: Spacecraft are engineering marvels, designed to resist the thrust of liftoff, as well as the reverse pressure of the void.

senses.definition: The primary effort; the goal.
senses.example: Ostensibly, the class was about public health in general, but the main thrust was really sex education.

senses.definition: To make advance with force.
senses.example: We thrust at the enemy with our forces.

senses.definition: To force something upon someone.
senses.example: I asked her not to thrust the responsibility on me.

senses.definition: To push out or extend rapidly or powerfully.
senses.example: He thrust his arm into the icy stream and grabbed a wriggling fish, astounding the observers.

senses.definition: To push or drive with force; to shove.
senses.example: to thrust anything with the hand or foot, or with an instrument

senses.definition: To enter by pushing; to squeeze in.
To stab; to pierce; usually with through.

core.definition: A strong, forceful push or lunge forward; also, the forward force an engine or jet produces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, and the th is voiceless as in 'think.' Keep the vowel short, like the u in 'cut', and do not add an extra vowel before the final st.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It can be aggressive when describing a physical attack, and neutral when describing engines or politics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thrust in everyday speech for a forceful push, and in technical speech for engine power, such as 'jet thrust.' In business and politics it means the main point or direction of an argument, as in 'the thrust of the proposal.' Phrases like 'the main thrust of' are natural in meetings and news.

distinctions.note: Push is the everyday word, while thrust suggests more force, sharpness or suddenness.
A lunge is a sudden movement of the body toward something, while a thrust can be a deliberate push or stab.

examples.everyday: He gave the broken gate a thrust with his shoulder and it finally opened.
examples.professional: The main thrust of my proposal is to cut the data pipeline's latency by half.
examples.analytical: The author's central thrust is that moral authority depends on humility rather than power.

nuance.analogy: Like a rocket engine that pushes everything forward, a thrust is a steady or sudden force driving motion in one direction.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English thrusten, from Old Norse þrýsta, to press or squeeze.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, saying 'thr-us-ta' or 'THRUST-uh.'
Using thrust as a verb in the noun sense, as in 'the thrust of the policy' is fine but 'I thrust the idea' is less natural than 'I pushed the idea.'

thrust.etymology: From Middle English *þristen*, from Old Norse *þrysta*, from Proto-Germanic **þrustijaną*, possibly from Proto-Indo-European **trewd-*.

senses.definition: A regularly-shaped slab of clay or other material, affixed to cover or decorate a surface, as in a roof-tile, glazed tile, stove tile, carpet tile, etc.
A rectangular graphic.
senses.example: Each tile within the map consists of 256 × 256 pixels.

senses.definition: Any of various flat cuboid playing pieces used in certain games, such as dominoes, Scrabble, or mahjong.
(Lego building) A Lego piece that is 1/3 the height of a brick, and is smooth without studs on top.
A stiff hat.
To cover with tiles.
senses.example: The handyman tiled the kitchen.

senses.definition: To arrange in a regular pattern, with adjoining edges (applied to tile-like objects, graphics, windows in a computer interface).
To optimize (a loop in program code) by means of the tiling technique.
To seal a lodge against intrusions from unauthorized people.
To protect from the intrusion of the uninitiated.
senses.example: to tile a Masonic lodge

core.definition: A thin, flat piece of ceramic, stone, or similar material used to cover floors, walls, or roofs.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables; the second is a syllabic l that sounds like 'uhl' with no separate vowel. Don't say 'tie-ELL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, everyday word in home and building talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tile' for floors, bathrooms, and kitchen backsplashes; 'ceramic tile' is a common phrase. A hardware store clerk might ask, 'What kind of tile are you looking for?' For roofs, Americans often say 'shingles' for asphalt and 'roof tiles' for clay or concrete tiles.

distinctions.note: A brick is a solid block of fired clay used in walls, while a tile is a thin slab used as a surface covering.
Carpet is a soft textile floor covering, while tile is hard, flat, and easy to clean.

examples.everyday: We're going to put new tile in the kitchen this summer.
examples.professional: The contractor priced the bathroom job by the square foot of tile.
examples.analytical: The mosaic's meaning depends on how each tile contributes to a larger pattern, which the viewer perceives only from a distance.

nuance.analogy: Like a single square in a checkerboard that completes the whole board.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'tegula', meaning roof tile, from 'tegere', to cover.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'tile' with a long e as 'TEEL'; it rhymes with 'mile'.
Using 'tile' for an asphalt roof; Americans usually say 'shingles' for that.

tile.etymology: From Middle English *tile,tyl,tigel,tiȝel,teȝele*, from Old English *tiġele,tieġle,tiġle* (“tile, brick”), from **tigulā* (“tile, brick”), from Proto-Germanic **tigulǭ* (“tile, brick”), from Latin *tēgula*, from Proto-Indo-European **teg-* (“to cover”).

senses.definition: The amount of time an algorithm requires to run, as a function of the amount of input, measured in such a way as to ignore constant terms and multiplication by constant terms.

core.definition: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as its input grows, written in Big O notation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TIME first, then PLEK in complexity, and the -ity ending is a reduced vowel. Many learners stress the -plex syllable incorrectly or pronounce the final syllable as 'tee' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers and computer science students use this term constantly in interviews and code reviews. Say 'the time complexity is linear' or 'this is O of n squared' in conversation. Often it is paired with space complexity.

distinctions.note: Time complexity measures how running time grows with input size, while space complexity measures how much memory the algorithm needs.

examples.everyday: My nephew is studying for coding interviews and keeps asking me what time complexity means.
examples.professional: Before we merge this change, can you check the time complexity of the sorting step? It may slow down large batches.
examples.analytical: The proof establishes an upper bound on time complexity, though it says nothing about the constant factors that dominate in practice.

nuance.analogy: Time complexity is like a commute estimate: it describes how the travel time grows as you add more stops, not the exact minutes on a given day.
nuance.etymology: Compound of time (Old English tima) and complexity (from Latin complexus, interwoven).
common_mistakes: Confusing time complexity with actual running time in seconds, which depends on hardware.
Stressing complexity on the wrong syllable, as in 'kum-PLEX-i-tee' with the wrong vowel.

senses.definition: Of or relating to topology.
Equipped with a topology that is typically required to be compatible with the underlying structure in some way.
senses.example: topological group

core.definition: Relating to topology, the branch of mathematics that studies properties of shapes that stay the same when the shape is stretched or bent without tearing.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LAH, the third syllable. Many learners put the stress on 'top'; keep the 'o' in the middle reduced, and say the final syllable as a light 'kuhl'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and data scientists use topological to describe properties or spaces studied in topology. Outside math, Americans might use it loosely, as in 'a topological view of networks,' but the word is strongly tied to its technical meaning. In casual conversation it may sound too specialized.

distinctions.note: Topographical refers to the surface features of land on a map, while topological refers to abstract properties of shapes or spaces that survive continuous deformation.
Geometric properties depend on exact distances and angles, while topological properties depend only on how points are connected and continuity.

examples.everyday: My brother studies math, and he says a coffee mug and a donut are topologically the same because each has one hole.
examples.professional: We used a topological method to show that the clusters in the dataset keep their structure after the transformation.
examples.analytical: The proof depends on a topological argument about continuity, which does not require any notion of distance.

nuance.analogy: Topological properties are like the features of a rubber sheet that survive stretching: you can bend the sheet, but you cannot cut or glue it.
nuance.etymology: From topology, combined with the suffix -al, from Greek topos (place) and logos (study).
common_mistakes: Confusing topological with topographical, which refers to land surfaces on maps.
Putting the stress on the first syllable, as TOP-uh-LOJ-ik-ul.

senses.definition: Complaining about heavy traffic.

core.definition: A common complaint that road traffic is very heavy, slow or stalled, used to explain delay or frustration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TRAF and TEHR. The word 'is' is weak and reduces to 'iz' or 'z', and 'traffic is' links smoothly into 'TRAF-i-kiz'. The second syllable of 'terrible' is a weak schwa and the final -ble is 'bul'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and complaining, but usually light and sociable in small talk. It signals frustration, not anger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this as small talk when arriving late or meeting someone on the road. Typical replies include 'Tell me about it' or 'Yeah, it was a nightmare.' If you want to be more polite, say 'Sorry, traffic was really bad.' It is informal and fits conversations with friends, coworkers and neighbors.

distinctions.note: Bad is milder and more neutral, while terrible is stronger and more emotional in everyday American speech.

distinctions.vs: There is a lot of traffic.
distinctions.note: This is a neutral observation, while 'Traffic is terrible' adds a complaint and invites sympathy.

collocations: I hate it when traffic is terrible.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, traffic is terrible on the freeway this morning.
examples.professional: Traffic is terrible around the stadium, so let's move the meeting to the video call.
examples.analytical: When people say traffic is terrible, they often describe a shared experience of lost time rather than a technical measure of flow.

nuance.analogy: Saying traffic is terrible is like a weather report for the road: it tells listeners what kind of day to expect.
nuance.etymology: Traffic comes from Italian traffico; terrible comes from Latin terribilis, 'frightening, causing fear'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'terrible' with a strong final vowel, as in 'TEHR-uh-BULL'.
Saying 'the traffic are terrible', because traffic is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

conversation.text: Traffic is terrible this morning, so I'll be a few minutes late.
"How was the drive?" "Traffic is terrible on the bridge."
Traffic is terrible around here at five; let's leave earlier.

senses.definition: The act or process of transcribing, or converting spoken (or sometimes signed) language to the written form.
Something that has been transcribed.
senses.example: These frame tale interludes frequently include transcriptions of Italian folk songs.

senses.definition: A recorded radio or television program.
A representation of speech sounds as phonetic symbols.
Synonym of copywork.
The synthesis of RNA under the direction of DNA.
An adaptation of a composition.
senses.example: These frame tale interludes frequently include transcriptions of Italian folk songs.

core.definition: The act of converting spoken or recorded language into written text, or the written text produced by that process.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SKRIP, and the ending -tion sounds like 'shun'. The t in the middle is a clear t, not a flap, because it comes before a stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a routine professional task.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, transcription is common in medicine, law, journalism and research. In radio and television, it can also mean a recorded program, though that sense is less common in everyday talk. Americans usually say transcript for the finished written document.

distinctions.note: Transcription is the process or act of converting speech to text. A transcript is the finished written record.
Transcription changes sound into writing in the same language, while translation changes the language itself.

examples.everyday: The app's transcription of my voice memo was almost perfect.
examples.professional: The transcription vendor needs the audio files by noon so the report can go out on time.
examples.analytical: A careful transcription preserves hesitations and overlapping speech that a clean summary would erase.

nuance.analogy: A transcription is like a photograph of a conversation: it holds the words but not the tone of voice.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transcriptio, from transcribere 'to copy over'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as TRAN-skrip-shun.
Confusing transcription with translation.
Using transcription for a finished document, where transcript is the better word.

transcription.etymology: From Middle French *transcription*, or directly from Latin *transcriptiōnem*, from *trānscrībō* (“transcribe”).

senses.definition: A medieval siege engine consisting of a large pivoting arm heavily weighted on one end.
senses.example: Medieval trebuchets are said to have been capable of launching 90-kg projectiles over distances of more than 300 meters.

senses.definition: A torture device for dunking suspected witches by means of a chair attached to the end of a long pole.
To shoot with a trebuchet.

core.definition: A large medieval siege machine that uses a heavy counterweight on a swinging arm to hurl stones or other objects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TREB. The middle syllable is a quick 'yuh' or 'yoo', and the final syllable rhymes with 'bet' with a light French-derived ending. Americans often say it with the stress on TREB and a short final vowel.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a historical or game-related term, sometimes used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trebuchet mostly in history, military history, or video game and fantasy contexts. The second meaning, a ducking chair for suspected witches, is historical and rare, so most learners need only the siege engine sense. Using the verb form is uncommon outside historical writing.

distinctions.note: A catapult usually uses torsion or tension to launch projectiles, while a trebuchet uses a falling counterweight to swing its arm.
A ballista is a crossbow-like machine that shoots bolts, while a trebuchet throws heavy projectiles in an arc.

collocations: launch a stone from a trebuchet

examples.everyday: My son built a model trebuchet out of popsicle sticks for his science fair project.
examples.professional: For the game's history module, the designers modeled the siege trebuchet's counterweight so the animation matches real physics.
examples.analytical: The trebuchet changed medieval warfare because its counterweight let attackers hurl heavy stones much farther than earlier catapults.

nuance.analogy: Think of a playground seesaw where a heavy bucket drops on one end to fling a ball out the other end.
nuance.etymology: From French 'trébuchet', a balance or a small trap, from Old French 'trebuchier', to overturn.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, saying 'treb-yoo-SHAY'.
Confusing it with catapult, which works on a different principle.

senses.definition: Awe-inspiring; terrific.
Notable for its size, power, or excellence.
senses.example: Van Beethoven's ninth symphony is a tremendous piece of music.

senses.definition: Extremely large (in amount, extent, degree, etc.) or great.
senses.example: There was a tremendous outpouring of support.

core.definition: Very large, great, or excellent; impressive enough to be exciting or remarkable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN, the second syllable. The first vowel is a short reduced 'ih', and the final syllable is a reduced 'us', not 'ous' as a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: positive in everyday use, meaning excellent or amazing; neutral or negative when it means huge in a bad way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tremendous to praise something great, like 'a tremendous help' or 'a tremendous effort', and it can sound enthusiastic. In casual talk people often prefer 'awesome', 'huge', or 'great'. It can also mean enormous, as in a tremendous amount of work.

distinctions.note: Huge describes size, while tremendous can describe size, quality, or impact, often with more praise.
Awesome is very casual and overused; tremendous is more formal and sounds sincere.

examples.everyday: Thanks for watching the kids last night, that was a tremendous help.
examples.professional: The team put in a tremendous effort to meet the launch deadline, and the results show it.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that the tremendous mystery of God exceeds every human category, yet is revealed in Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a towering mountain that makes you stop and stare, something tremendous overwhelms you with its scale or quality.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'tremendus', to be trembled at, from Latin 'tremere', to tremble.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying 'TREM-en-dus'.
Using tremendous for ordinary things where great or good fits better.

senses.definition: The condition of being tribal.
A feeling of identity and loyalty to one's tribe.

The tendency among human beings to form socially cohesive groups within which there exists social pressure upon the individual to conform to either common behaviors, customs, habits, mores and/or norms, and which groups exhibit greater or lesser degrees of exclusivism.

core.definition: The tendency to form close-knit groups, feel strong loyalty to one's own group, and often distrust or exclude outsiders.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TRY. The middle syllable -bə- is a weak schwa, so don't say it as 'bay'; the final -ism is a short, unstressed 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative or critical, since it describes loyalty that excludes or hostility toward outsiders. It can be neutral in anthropology or sociology, where it describes a social pattern without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in political commentary, social science, and conversations about identity, often when describing partisan or group loyalty that blocks cooperation. Calling someone tribal in a casual conversation can sound like an insult, so be careful with it. In anthropology it simply refers to the social structure of traditional communities.

distinctions.note: Clannishness is a narrower term for a family-like closeness that keeps outsiders at a distance, while tribalism is broader and often describes political or cultural group identity.
Patriotism is love of one's country and is usually viewed positively, while tribalism stresses group loyalty that can exclude or oppose others.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of how much tribalism there is online; everybody just picks a side and attacks the other one.
examples.professional: Our product team has too much tribalism, so the data people and the engineers rarely share their work with each other.
examples.analytical: Tribalism arises when group identity becomes the primary lens through which individuals evaluate truth, morality, and the motives of others.

nuance.analogy: Tribalism is like a sports fan section that cheers for its own team so hard that it treats the other side's fans as enemies, even when they share the same stadium.
nuance.etymology: From 'tribe' (Latin tribus, one of the three original divisions of the Roman people) plus the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'tree' instead of 'try'.
Using tribalism to mean a neutral cultural difference, when it usually implies exclusion or hostility.

senses.definition: A Roman Catholic philosophy that emphasizes the prerogatives and powers of the Pope.

core.definition: In Roman Catholicism, the view that papal authority should be broad and supreme, especially in governing the universal church and its teaching.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on MAHN, the third syllable. The word has a weak middle syllable so say it quickly; the ending -ism is weak, so pronounce it -iz-um rather than a strong ism.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship but can be heard as negative when used by critics to describe rigid Church centralization.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ultramontanism almost only in church history, theology and Catholic studies. It can be a loaded term: supporters see it as faithful loyalty to the papacy, while critics see it as centralized control. In ordinary conversation people would say 'strong papal authority' or 'very pope-centered Catholicism.'

distinctions.note: Papalism is a broader term for support of papal power; ultramontanism specifically refers to the 19th-century movement favoring papal authority over national or local churches.
Gallicanism asserted the rights of national churches and kings against the pope, so it is the opposing position to ultramontanism.

examples.everyday: My history professor said that the 19th century saw a strong rise of ultramontanism, when the pope's authority became much more central.
examples.professional: Our seminar paper will trace how ultramontanism shaped Vatican policy and the definition of papal infallibility at the First Vatican Council.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether ultramontanism was a response to modern secularism or the logical development of a medieval papal claim to universal jurisdiction.

nuance.analogy: Ultramontanism is like a central headquarters that insists every branch must follow its orders directly, rather than letting regional offices decide.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ultra montes 'beyond the mountains', referring to Rome as seen from northern Europe, plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing ultramontanism with ultramontane, which is the adjective or person; the noun is ultramontanism.
Pronouncing the stress on the final syllable; the stress is on MAHN.

traditions.view: Ultramontanism is a historical emphasis on full papal authority, and many Catholics regard the papacy's primacy and teaching role, including infallibility as defined in 1870, as an expression of the church's unity.

Eastern Orthodox Christians generally reject papal supremacy as a universal jurisdiction, holding that authority is shared among bishops and councils and that Rome's role is one of honor among equals.

Most Protestants reject ultramontanism, arguing that Scripture, not papal authority, is the final rule of faith, though Lutherans, Anglicans and Reformed churches differ in how much authority they grant to church councils and bishops.

senses.definition: Not biased.
Impartial or without bias or prejudice.

core.definition: Fair and impartial, not favoring one side, or based on objective information without bias.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BY, the second syllable. The final -ased sounds like ust, with a reduced vowel, and the d is not pronounced separately.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals fairness and objectivity, which Americans value in research, journalism, and workplace decisions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unbiased in professional, academic, and news contexts, such as 'an unbiased sample' or 'an unbiased judge.' In everyday speech people often say 'fair' or 'neutral.' In statistics, unbiased has a precise technical meaning, so use it carefully when discussing estimators.

distinctions.note: Impartial focuses on fair judgment in a dispute, while unbiased focuses on the absence of a tilt or prejudice in the process or information.
Objective describes facts and standards that do not depend on personal feelings, while unbiased describes the absence of a particular lean in a person or method.

examples.everyday: Can you give me an unbiased opinion on whether this restaurant is actually worth the price?
examples.professional: We need an unbiased sample from all regions, so the model does not overrepresent one customer segment.
examples.analytical: A philosopher might argue that no inquirer can be fully unbiased, yet a method can still be designed to correct for predictable distortions.

nuance.analogy: An unbiased judgment is like a scale that is level before anything is placed on it, so the reading reflects only the weight.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus biased, from bias, from French biais, meaning slant or oblique.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as un-BY-as-ed with an extra syllable, when the ending is usually one syllable.
Using unbiased to mean neutral in every sense, when statistics has a precise meaning for an estimator whose expected value equals the true parameter.

senses.definition: Without ceasing (stopping); continuously.

core.definition: Continuously, without stopping or pausing for any length of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE, and the final -ly is a light 'lee' sound. The first syllable is reduced to 'uh', so do not say 'un-SEES'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often expresses dedication or persistence, though it can describe a wearying repetition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unceasingly in writing, speeches, and formal descriptions. In conversation they would more likely say nonstop, all the time, or constantly. It is common in news reports and tributes describing someone's tireless work.

distinctions.note: Constantly is everyday and neutral, while unceasingly is more formal and stresses unbroken continuity.
Continually often means repeatedly with breaks, while unceasingly means without any break at all.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has been talking unceasingly about her trip to Italy.
examples.professional: The support engineers worked unceasingly through the outage until the service was restored.
examples.analytical: Paul writes that he prays unceasingly for his readers, showing a pattern of constant intercession in the early church.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock's second hand: it moves steadily and never skips a tick.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'unceasing' with the adverb suffix '-ly', from Old French 'cesser' and Latin 'cessare' meaning to stop.
common_mistakes: Using unceasingly in casual speech where constantly or nonstop sounds more natural.
Stressing the final syllable instead of SEE.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is adialeiptōs (ἀδιαλείπτως), the adverb from adialeiptos, meaning without interruption. Paul uses it in Romans 1:9 for remembering the Roman church in prayer. In 1 Thessalonians 1:3 he says he remembers their work of faith and labor of love unceasingly before God. In Acts 12:5 the church prays earnestly for Peter while he is in prison.

senses.definition: Inflexible and unwilling to negotiate or make concessions.
Principled.

core.definition: Refusing to accept lower standards or give ground in an argument; firm and inflexible about principles or demands.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on KAHM, with a lighter secondary stress on -MY-. The middle syllable reduces to a quick uh, and the r in the second syllable is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It can praise firm principles or criticize rigidity, so context decides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for people or organizations that hold firm standards, in work, sports, politics and reviews. It often appears as uncompromising standards or uncompromising commitment, which are praise. Describing a person as uncompromising can also suggest stubbornness, so use it with care in personal conversations.

distinctions.note: Stubborn is usually a personal trait and often negative; uncompromising can praise firm principles as well as criticize rigidity.
Inflexible stresses an inability to adapt to changing circumstances; uncompromising stresses refusal to give up principles or demands.

examples.everyday: My mom is uncompromising about homework, so we always finish it before anything else.
examples.professional: Our QA lead is uncompromising on test coverage, so we never ship code without it.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics is uncompromising in holding that moral duties bind regardless of their consequences.

nuance.analogy: Like a steel bridge that will not bend: it keeps its shape under any load.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus compromising, from Latin compromittere, to agree mutually to abide by arbitration.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the middle syllable or on -MI-, instead of KAHM at the start of the root.
Using uncompromising to mean just unwilling to talk; it implies firm principles or standards.

senses.definition: Not feigned.
Genuine.
Not false or hypocritical.

core.definition: Genuine and sincere; real, not pretended, false, or put on for show.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAYND, and the g in feign is silent. The word rhymes with pained and rained, not with fine or feline.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive, suggesting sincerity and absence of hypocrisy. It is most often used to praise feelings, gratitude, or faith.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use unfeigned in conversation; it appears in formal letters, speeches, sermons, and literary writing. Everyday speakers would say sincere, genuine, or heartfelt instead. Using unfeigned in casual speech would sound old-fashioned or deliberately elevated.

distinctions.note: Sincere is common in everyday speech; unfeigned is more formal and emphasizes the absence of any pretense.
Genuine can describe objects or feelings; unfeigned is used mainly for feelings, character, and faith.
Heartfelt is warm and everyday; unfeigned is more formal and stresses that nothing false is mixed in.

examples.everyday: Thank you for the card; your unfeigned kindness meant more to me than you know.
examples.professional: The board's unfeigned interest in the project surprised me, since they had been skeptical in earlier meetings.
examples.analytical: Paul asks his readers for love that is unfeigned, which implies that love must be sincere and not a performance of kindness.

nuance.analogy: Unfeigned feeling is like real gold rather than gold-colored paint: the true thing has nothing hidden underneath.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus feigned, from Old French feindre, from Latin fingere (to shape, form, pretend).
common_mistakes: Confusing feign (to pretend) with feint (a move meant to deceive) or with fine.
Using unfeigned in casual speech, where sincere or genuine sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word anypokritos (without hypocrisy, genuine) is translated unfeigned in older English versions. Romans 12:9 calls for love that is genuine, and 2 Corinthians 6:6 lists genuine love among marks of Paul's ministry. Both passages stress that the believer's love must be real and not a pretense.

senses.definition: Cause to become one; make into a unit; consolidate; merge; combine.
Become one.

core.definition: To bring separate people, groups or things together so that they become one whole or act as one.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, YOO. The ending -fy rhymes with 'sky', and the middle syllable is a quick, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests harmony, cooperation and a shared purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unify in politics, business and organizations, as in 'unify the team' or 'unify our systems.' In casual talk, people often say 'bring together' or 'get everyone on the same page'. It is usually used with an object: unify something.

distinctions.note: Combine is a general word for putting things together, while unify emphasizes making them one coherent whole.
Merge often refers to companies, files or lanes of traffic and usually means joining two things into one, while unify emphasizes common purpose or consistency.

examples.everyday: The holiday dinner really unified the family after a tense year.
examples.professional: Our goal this quarter is to unify the three reporting tools into one dashboard.
examples.analytical: Her argument is that a shared moral vocabulary can unify citizens who disagree about policy.

nuance.analogy: To unify is like weaving separate threads into one cloth, so they hold together.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'unificare', from 'unus' (one) and '-ficare' (make).
common_mistakes: Using 'unify' with 'with' as in 'unify with'; the usual pattern is 'unify something' or 'unify around something'.
Pronouncing the middle as a full 'ah' vowel instead of a reduced schwa.

senses.definition: Not able to be measured; immeasurable.

core.definition: Impossible to measure, or so large or small that it cannot be measured accurately.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MEH. The 'zh' sound is like the 's' in 'measure', and the final -able is a reduced 'uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It often describes something vast or valuable beyond calculation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually use immeasurable or 'impossible to measure' in everyday talk. Unmeasurable is more common in technical and literary writing, especially in statistics or philosophy. It is not a strong daily word, but it is correct.

distinctions.note: Immeasurable is more common in everyday and literary English and emphasizes vastness. Unmeasurable is more neutral and technical.
Unmeasured means it has not been measured yet, but it could be. Unmeasurable means it cannot be measured at all.

examples.everyday: The sunset over the lake had an unmeasurable beauty that no photo could capture.
examples.professional: Some of the project's benefits, like team trust, are unmeasurable with our current metrics.
examples.analytical: Theologians have argued that God's grace is unmeasurable by any human standard of merit.

nuance.analogy: An unmeasurable quantity is like the depth of the ocean from a small rowboat: you know it is there, but no ruler can reach its bottom.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus measurable, from measure, from Latin mensura.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'mesh-ur' with no 'zh' sound.
Using it when the thing is merely unknown; unmeasurable means it cannot be measured in principle.

senses.definition: The property of being unwilling.

core.definition: The state of not wanting to do something, or of being reluctant to act or agree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on WIL. The final syllable 'ness' is short and reduced, and the 'ing' is pronounced with a clear 'ing' sound rather than 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a reasonable hesitation or an obstinate refusal, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in formal or professional settings, such as explaining why a deal stalled or why someone is resisting a change. In casual speech they more often say 'they didn't want to' or 'they weren't into it.' It works well in news reporting and in workplace discussions.

distinctions.note: Reluctance is a feeling of hesitation; unwillingness is a broader stance of not wanting to act at all.
Refusal is an explicit statement of 'no'; unwillingness can be a quiet state that never gets stated.

examples.everyday: Her unwillingness to talk about the accident made us worry even more.
examples.professional: The team's unwillingness to adopt the new tool is slowing down the migration.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats the human unwillingness to love God as a deeper problem than mere ignorance of the truth.

nuance.analogy: Unwillingness is like a locked door with no handle on the inside: the person is there, but nothing is going to open it.
nuance.etymology: From 'unwilling' (not willing), plus the suffix '-ness,' which turns an adjective into a noun.
common_mistakes: Saying 'unwillingless' or misspelling the double 'l' in 'unwilling' as one 'l'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ness' with a long e sound.

senses.definition: Random variable.
A measurable quantity capable of taking on a number of values.
A variable, often the set of x values plotted on a graph.
The measured magnitude of a variable.
To alter; to vary; to make or become different.

core.definition: In statistics, a random variable or a measurable quantity that can take on a range of values.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending is a short "it." As a verb, it is pronounced "VAIR-ee-ayt," so be careful to match the form to the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use variate mainly in statistics and mathematics textbooks, and in papers on probability. Many Americans would say random variable or simply variable instead, since variate is less common in everyday technical use. In the verb sense, it is archaic or literary, so people would more likely say vary.

distinctions.note: Variable is the usual term in statistics and mathematics; variate is more specialized and less common, often used in older or more formal texts.
A random variable is the precise technical name for a variable whose value depends on chance; variate is a shorter term for the same idea in some texts.

examples.everyday: I don't use the word variate much, but my statistics friend uses it to mean a random quantity.
examples.professional: The simulation generates a random variate from the distribution at each step.
examples.analytical: A variate in a probability model is best understood as a function that assigns numerical values to outcomes of a random process.

nuance.analogy: A variate is like a dice roll recorded as a number: the process is uncertain, but each result is a value you can measure.
nuance.etymology: From Latin variatus, past participle of variare, to change.
common_mistakes: Using variate for an everyday variable without a technical purpose, where variable is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the ending as "ayt" when used as a noun.
Confusing the noun and verb pronunciations.

senses.definition: Commanding respect because of age, dignity, character or position.
Worthy of reverence.
Ancient, antiquated or archaic.
Made sacred especially by religious or historical association.
Giving an impression of aged goodness and benevolence.

core.definition: Deserving respect because of age, wisdom, dignity, character, or long service, especially in a community or institution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, VEN. The second and third syllables are reduced, and the final 'ble' is a syllabic 'l' in American speech, so it sounds like 'bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies respect earned through age, service, or character, and it can sound slightly old-fashioned when used of ordinary people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use venerable for institutions, traditions, and elders: 'a venerable university' or 'a venerable professor.' It is formal and often used in writing or speeches. In casual talk, old or respected is more natural. Be careful when describing things, since venerable can also mean old-fashioned, which may sound odd in praise of a new product.

distinctions.note: Old is neutral and only states age; venerable adds respect and dignity earned over time.
Respected describes general regard, while venerable suggests reverence and a long, honored history.

examples.everyday: That diner has been on Main Street for seventy years, and everyone treats it like a venerable local landmark.
examples.professional: The venerable firm still uses its original review process, which is both its strength and its bottleneck.
examples.analytical: Aquinas calls the tradition venerable because it preserves the wisdom of earlier generations, though he still subjects it to rational examination.

nuance.analogy: A venerable person is like an old oak tree: its age and endurance command respect without any effort to impress.
nuance.etymology: From Latin venerabilis, from venerari, 'to revere'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in vuh-NAIR-uh-bul.
Using venerable for any old object in praise; it implies respect, not just age.

venerable.etymology: From Middle French *vénérable*, from Old French, from Latin *venerabilis*.

senses.definition: The fine arts as a subject of study or expertise; understanding of arts and antiquities.
Objets d'art collectively.
Especially with reference to the writings of Machiavelli (1469–1527): the requisite qualities for political or military success; vitality, determination; power.
Moral worth; virtue, virtuousness.

core.definition: Appreciation and knowledge of fine arts and antiquities, or the collection of objects valued for their artistic quality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, 'too', which is a borrowing from Italian. The first syllable is a weak 'ver' with the r pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it sounds learned and refined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this word mainly in art history, museum studies and antiques writing. Most Americans would say 'fine arts', 'antiquities' or 'objects of art' in everyday speech. In Machiavelli scholarship, 'virtù' names political skill or vigor, a sense that is rarely used outside that field.

distinctions.note: 'Virtue' means moral goodness or a good quality of character, while 'virtu' means artistic knowledge or the objects themselves.
A 'virtuoso' is a highly skilled performer, while 'virtu' refers to art knowledge or objects rather than a person's skill.

examples.everyday: At the estate auction, the dealer praised the collection's virtu to the guests.
examples.professional: The curator's catalog entry explains the bronzes' value as objects of virtu from the Renaissance.
examples.analytical: In Machiavelli's writing, virtù names the quality that lets a ruler master fortune, not moral goodness.

nuance.analogy: Virtu is like a museum's sense of taste: knowing what is beautiful, old and valuable.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'virtù', from Latin 'virtus' (manliness, excellence, courage).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'virtu' with 'virtue', which means moral goodness.
Stressing the first syllable, 'VUR-too', rather than the Italian-style final stress.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to volume or volumes.
Consisting of many folds, coils, or convolutions.
Of great volume, or bulk; large.
Having written much, or produced many volumes.
senses.example: a voluminous writer

core.definition: Very large in quantity, size, or volume; taking up a great deal of space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO, and the second syllable is a weak schwa. The -ous ending is pronounced like uhs, not a full oo-sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe impressive large amounts or, in a complaint, something overwhelming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use voluminous in formal writing and descriptions of large amounts of text, records, or clothing. In everyday speech they say huge, a lot of, or bulky. It appears often in legal and academic writing, for example voluminous records or voluminous correspondence.

distinctions.note: Large is common and neutral about size; voluminous specifically refers to great volume or bulk, often of papers, fabric, or writing.
Vast emphasizes immense extent or scale, while voluminous stresses a large amount that fills or fills out a space.

examples.everyday: She wore a voluminous coat that made her look twice her size.
examples.professional: The auditors reviewed voluminous transaction logs before they found the duplicated payments.
examples.analytical: Her voluminous footnotes demonstrate a mastery of the sources, but they also distract from the central claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a suitcase stuffed with clothes that barely closes: the amount is large enough to fill the whole space.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin voluminosus, from volumen, roll or volume.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as vuh-LOO-muh-NUS; the -ous ending is weak.
Confusing voluminous with voluptuous, which means curvy or sensually pleasing, not large in amount.

senses.definition: A thin disk of consecrated unleavened bread used in communion.
A light, thin, flat biscuit/cookie.
A soft disk originally made of flour, and later of gelatin or a similar substance, used to seal letters, attach papers etc.
A thin disk of silicon or other semiconductor on which an electronic circuit is produced.
To seal or fasten with a wafer.

core.definition: A thin, flat disk of unleavened bread consecrated and eaten during Communion or the Lord's Supper in some churches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'er' is a light American r-colored vowel. Do not pronounce the 'a' as 'ah'; it is a long 'ay' sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral; in church contexts it is sacred, and in food contexts it is a plain, ordinary item.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, you will hear 'wafer' or 'communion wafer' in Catholic and some Lutheran, Episcopal, or Methodist services. Many Protestant churches use bread cubes or pieces instead. Outside church, Americans use 'wafer' for a thin crisp cookie, such as a vanilla wafer, which is probably the sense you will meet most often in stores.

distinctions.note: In Catholic usage, host is the consecrated bread used in Mass, often a wafer, while wafer is the more general term for the thin disk itself.
A cracker is a dry, usually salty snack, while a wafer is thin and sweet or delicate, and a communion wafer is specifically consecrated.

examples.everyday: At the store, I grabbed a box of vanilla wafers to go with my tea.
examples.professional: Our church ordered communion wafers from a supplier that makes them unleavened and gluten-free.
examples.analytical: In Exodus 29, unleavened wafers anointed with oil are part of the priestly offering, which gives the later Eucharistic wafer a biblical root.

nuance.analogy: A communion wafer is like a thin, plain signpost pointing to a much larger meaning: the simple bread carries the weight of the sacrament.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'waufre,' from Old French 'waufre' or 'gaufre,' a honeycomb-patterned cake or pastry.
common_mistakes: Confusing the communion wafer with the cookie sense in a church conversation; context usually makes it clear.
Pronouncing it 'WAH-fer' with an open a sound instead of the American 'WAY-fer.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'raqiq' means a thin cake or wafer, and Exodus 29:2 and Leviticus 8:26 describe unleavened wafers offered in priestly rites. The Greek word 'azymos' means unleavened, and the Gospel accounts of the Last Supper, such as Matthew 26:26, describe Jesus blessing bread, which later Christians connected with wafers. These passages show the ritual background for the wafer used in Communion.

traditions.view: The Church uses unleavened wafer bread, which is consecrated at Mass and believed to become the body of Christ through transubstantiation.
Orthodox churches use leavened bread, prepared as prosphora or similar loaves, and do not use unleavened wafers for the Eucharist.

Practice varies: Lutheran, Anglican, and some Reformed churches often use wafers or bread, while many Baptist and Pentecostal churches use bread cubes or whole loaves and emphasize memorial or spiritual presence rather than transubstantiation.

wafer.etymology: From Middle English *wafre*, from Anglo-Norman *wafre*, *waufre*, from a Germanic source.

senses.definition: To help to swallow (something, especially food or a pill) by drinking a liquid.
senses.example: Now we just need a drink to wash it down.

senses.definition: To wash (something) completely from top to bottom.
senses.example: You must wash the wall down well before painting.

senses.definition: To send (something) down the drain by washing action.
senses.example: There was some food residue in the sink, so she washed it down.

core.definition: To help swallow food or a pill by drinking a liquid, or to clean something thoroughly from top to bottom.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short o sound in 'wash', the American cot vowel, and stress 'down' as the main word. Link the phrase so it sounds like 'wahsh-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes everyday actions like taking medicine or cleaning a surface.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'wash down' most often for pills or food, as in 'He washed down the pills with a glass of water.' For cleaning, people more often say 'hose down' or 'scrub down' for surfaces. Note that 'wash down' is informal and mostly spoken, so in writing people may choose 'swallow' or 'clean.'

distinctions.note: Swallow only means to take food or liquid into the throat, while wash down adds the idea of drinking a liquid to help it go down.
Hose down means spraying with water from a hose, while wash down can mean cleaning by any washing action.

examples.everyday: I took two ibuprofen and washed them down with a big glass of water.
examples.professional: Before the client visit, the cleaning crew washed down the conference room and the glass walls.
examples.analytical: The phrasal verb 'wash down' combines the idea of cleansing with the sense of helping something pass down the throat.

nuance.analogy: Washing down a pill is like sending a bus down a road with a flood of water: the liquid carries the solid along.
nuance.etymology: 'Wash' from Old English 'wascan' plus 'down', meaning from a higher place to a lower one.
common_mistakes: Using 'wash down' without an object, like 'He washed down' with no pill or food named.
Confusing the particle: 'wash down' is not 'wash up' for cleaning dishes in American speech.

conversation.text: He washed down his burger with a big soda.
I need something to wash down this spicy food.
She washed the pill down with some water.

senses.definition: To relax; to get rid of stress; to destress.
senses.example: After a long day at work, she winds down by kickboxing.

senses.definition: To shut down slowly (by degrees or in phases).
senses.example: A program as complex as the Space Shuttle program takes some time to wind down.

senses.definition: To lower by winding, as with a crank or windlass.
senses.example: Wind down the car window if you want to talk to me.

senses.definition: To unwind.
senses.example: You'd better wind down that wind-up toy before you take it apart, or pieces might go flying.

senses.definition: To slow, as if coming to an end; to become calmer or less busy.
senses.example: The festival seems to be winding down now.

core.definition: To gradually relax after a busy or stressful time, or to slowly reduce activity until it stops.

pronunciation.tip: Wind rhymes with 'mind', with a long i, not the wind that blows. The main stress is on down, so say wynd DOWN. The d at the end of wind is quick, and the two words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes calming down, though it can also describe a slow decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in everyday conversation: 'I need to wind down after work.' A common reply is 'Good idea, take it easy.' It can also describe a business or project slowing down, as in 'the company is winding down operations.' It is informal, so in formal writing use 'wind down' only for gradual reduction.

distinctions.note: Relax is general and can describe any rest; wind down suggests a gradual transition from activity to rest.
Unwind is a very close synonym in American speech and is equally common for relaxing after work.
Slow down describes reducing speed; wind down suggests a gradual calming or ending, often over time.

examples.everyday: After the kids are asleep, I like to wind down with a cup of tea and a book.
examples.professional: We will start to wind down the old server in phases over the next two weeks.
examples.analytical: The narrative slowly winds down after the climax, allowing the characters to reflect on what they have lost.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock slowly running down after its spring has been released, moving more and more gently until it stops.
nuance.etymology: Wind from Old English windan, to turn or twist; the phrasal verb is an English combination.
common_mistakes: Using it as one word or with 'up' by mistake; 'wind down' and 'wind up' have different meanings.
Pronouncing wind with a short i like the weather; here it rhymes with 'mind'.

conversation.text: I like to read before bed to wind down.
The party started winding down around midnight.
The company is winding down its operations in Europe.
How do you wind down after a stressful day?

core.definition: A personal name in the Hebrew Bible, borne by several men, including an overseer of David's wine cellars and a Benjamite and an Asaphite listed in the genealogies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ZAB, with a short a as in cab. The final syllable is pronounced like the word eye, so it sounds like ZAB-dy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name in scripture with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Zabdi mainly in Bible study or when reading the Old Testament genealogies and lists of David's officials. It is rare as a modern given name. Readers may confuse it with Zabad, so checking the father's name is helpful.

examples.everyday: When we read 1 Chronicles at church, the pastor pointed out Zabdi, who was in charge of the wine cellars.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan on David's administration, Zabdi appears as an official responsible for storage, so students should note his role.
examples.analytical: The appearance of Zabdi among David's officials shows how the Chronicler records administrative offices alongside family lines.

nuance.analogy: Zabdi is like a name on a company org chart, whose job title tells you what he did in the household of the king.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Zavdi, probably meaning my gift, from a root meaning to bestow.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as dee instead of dy.
Mixing up Zabdi with Zabad, a different name in the same books.
nuance.biblical_note: Zabdi appears in several places. In 1 Chronicles 27:27 he is the Shiphmite who was over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars during David's reign. In 1 Chronicles 8:19 Zabdi is a son of Shimei in the tribe of Benjamin. In Joshua 7:1 Achan is identified as descended from Zabdi through Zerah, a family line that makes Zabdi an ancestor of the man who took devoted things at Jericho.
